The widest kill measured took **7** connections' slots, which on a nine-seat table is seven of the eight peers at once. **Two honest limits on this reading, both stated before anyone leans on it.** The reaper is **bounded**: `kill_nonused_tcp` returns early unless the number of connected relays exceeds `RECOMMENDED_FRIEND_TCP_CONNECTIONS`, and kills at most the excess — so it is a ceiling on relays, not a scythe, and a peer keeps the recommended count. And **this run is not a controlled comparison**: it also deadlocked — nine seats seated, nine in the group, **0 of 9 finishing a hand in 420 s**, which is `S1-AQ`'s deadlock reproduced under the stall and worse than the same recipe's previous outcome of 6 of 9. Whether the reaping is background noise present in every run or something the stall makes worse is **not answered here**, because every run carrying this instrument so far is a stalled one. A clean run with 0019 in the binary is the baseline that decides it, and it is owed before this reading goes any further. **THE BASELINE WAS TAKEN AT ONCE AND IT DECIDES IT — AGAINST THE READING ABOVE BEING A CAUSE.** `split144804-9`, the identical recipe with **no knob**: nine seated, nine in the group, **24 hands opened and 23 finished on every one of the nine nodes**, and **one** relay kill in the whole 420 seconds — at **419 s**, on one node, taking 7 slots. Against the stalled run's **12** kills from **39 s** onward on **seven** of nine nodes, 30 slots. So the reaping is emphatically **not** background: a healthy table reaps once, at the very end, and a stalled one reaps twelve times throughout. `tools/fold-relay-kills.py` prints exactly this comparison and says so when a run predates the instrument, rather than printing a zero. **And the direction is the thing this row must not get wrong again.** The obvious causal story — *the reaper takes the group's relays, so the handshake has nothing left* — has an equally good converse, and the converse is the likelier one: a group whose seats are not talking sends less, fewer slots therefore reach `ONLINE`, `lock_count` stays 0 on more relays, and `kill_nonused_tcp` reaps more of them. **On that reading the twelve kills are a symptom of the stall and not its cause**, and nothing measured here separates the two. What is **structural**, and independent of which way the arrow points, is the fact the instrument was built to expose: carrying out-of-band traffic for a `REGISTERED` slot never raises `lock_count`, so a relay doing precisely the job a first group handshake needs is *“nonused”* by the only function that decides that word. **That is a defect in a definition whether or not it caused this run.** **What would separate them**, stated so the next session does not have to re-derive it: the reaping is per-relay and the stall is per-seat, so a run in which the kills cluster on the stalled seat's `con_to` before its handshakes fail argues cause, and one in which they follow the table going quiet argues symptom. Patch 0020 is the half of that instrument this row was still missing — 0019's `slots_lost` counts an attachment at **any** status, so *“7 connections lose a slot”* cannot tell seven working out-of-band paths from seven attempts that never registered, and those two readings say opposite things. It now breaks the count down as `(%u online, %u registered, %u neither)`. **IT RAN, AND THE ANSWER IS AS UNAMBIGUOUS AS THIS ROW HAS EVER HAD.** `split150251-9`, the same stall recipe: **13 kills, 37 slots lost, and 37 of the 37 were `REGISTERED` — zero `online`, zero `neither`.** So the reaping is **not** abandoning attempts that had never connected: it takes **exactly** the out-of-band paths, which are the ones 0018 measured carrying group handshakes 135 times, and it takes nothing else. All thirteen are `status 2` with `lock_count 0`, on six of nine nodes, between 90 s and 250 s. **The defect is now measured end to end and the chain has no gaps left in it:** `kill_nonused_tcp` spares a relay only `if (onion \|\| lock_count > 0)`; `++lock_count` has one site and it is a slot reaching `ONLINE`; a `REGISTERED` slot is the only path a first group handshake has; and the slots actually taken are, measurably, **all `REGISTERED`**. **toxcore calls “nonused” a relay whose only slots are the ones doing the work.** **The causal direction is still not settled and this run does not settle it** — it deadlocked as well, 0 of 9 finishing, so the stall's quiet is still available as the explanation for why so many slots sat at `REGISTERED` rather than reaching `ONLINE`. What changed is that the **definition** defect no longer depends on the direction: whichever way the arrow points, a relay carrying out-of-band traffic is invisible to the only function that decides the word *used*. **And the stall's own reproducibility is now three runs deep**: 6 of 9 finishing under 0018, then 0 of 9 twice — against clean runs of the identical recipe at 26 and 23 hands finished on all nine nodes. **The candidate, named and NOT built.** Count a `REGISTERED` slot as use — either by sparing a relay any `con_to` holds a `REGISTERED` slot on, or by raising `lock_count` when a slot reaches `REGISTERED` rather than only `ONLINE`. It is local, has no wire format and no new state, and cannot lose compatibility with the public network because it only keeps a relay this peer already has. **It goes to a refutation pass before it goes into the tree, for the reason 0018 exists**: the last candidate this row was confident about was refuted by four independent readings on the same ground, and the one before that by the corpus. The obvious objection to answer first is relay economy — `RECOMMENDED_FRIEND_TCP_CONNECTIONS` is a **ceiling**, and a rule that spares every relay with a `REGISTERED` slot may simply stop the ceiling working. **AND WHILE THE PASS WAS RUNNING I REFUTED THE CANDIDATE'S MOTIVATION MYSELF, WHICH IS THE OUTCOME THIS ROW SHOULD HAVE EXPECTED.** The story the candidate rests on is *the reaper takes the `REGISTERED` slot, so the next group handshake has no path and fails*. If that were happening, a handshake failure would follow a kill **on the same node** more often than chance. **It does not.** Across the three runs carrying both instruments, **32 handshake failures and 2 of them fall within 30 s after a kill on that node — against 1.3 expected by chance.** No association at all. **And the counts point the other way outright.** The **clean** run `split144804-9` — 24 hands opened, 23 finished on all nine nodes — has **19** handshake failures and **one** relay kill. **Addendum, same day.** The last number the Tox question needed is on the status line. `tox_group_peer_join` fires exactly when `gconn->confirmed` flips, which is the flag `send_gc_lossless_packet_all_peers` requires — it skips a peer that is not confirmed and reports success anyway when there are none — so the set that callback reports is **precisely the set a broadcast reaches**. `Tox::peer_count` never checked that flag, which is why `group 3/3` was never proof of delivery and why every reading of that line had to hedge about it. The line now reads `group seen/confirmed/want`: **`seen > confirmed` is the library's skip happening, and the two agreeing rules it out** and leaves the three Rust-side discards — the latch above the publish, the trim that kept the wrong entry, and the early copy with no hold — as the whole explanation. **And on the first run that carried the instrument, they agree.** Ten seats: every node reported `group 9/9 confirmed/9` from the moment its group filled, on every status line. That does not prove the skip can never happen — it is real in the C and the incidence over a wider sample is still unmeasured — but on the runs this project actually makes, **`peer_count` and the confirmed set are the same number**, and the delivery hypothesis that survived yesterday's reading has nothing left to stand on.
| S1-AB | **`PROTOCOL.md` §13 and the code carry two different rendezvous constants under one name, which §14 says cannot happen.** §13 still defines `LOBBY_DERIVATION_STRING = "p2p-poker/mainline-lobby/v1"` and `LOBBY_INFOHASH = fd7c0d69…`, while `run::lobby_namespace` and the rewritten `NETWORK_STACK.md` §3.2 use `"p2p-poker/main-lobby/v1"` → the 34-byte multihash `12207e3429…`. `NETWORK_STACK.md` §14's own rule is *“no value has two names anywhere in the corpus”*; here one name has two values, which is the same defect read from the other end. **This is the one constant on which two independent implementations find each other or do not**, so it is not a tidying job. Found by the `S1-E` survey and not part of it.  **Fixed.** §13 now carries `LOBBY_DERIVATION_STRING = "p2p-poker/main-lobby/v1"` with its 34-byte `LOBBY_NAMESPACE_KEY`, and `RELAY_DERIVATION_STRING = "/libp2p/relay"` with its own — the multihash prefix `0x12 0x20` followed by `sha256(string)`, which is how go-libp2p's routing discovery keys a namespace. The `_INFOHASH` names go with the mechanism that had infohashes. **This was a correction and not a decision**, which is why it did not wait for the owner: the code has shipped these bytes since `56b0b50`, `NETWORK_STACK.md` §3.2 already documented them, and `the_lobby_rendezvous_key_is_the_published_one` already pinned them by asserting the literal bytes rather than recomputing them. §13 was the only place still carrying the old pair, and `corpus_constants` passes either way because it checks the constants the code exports — which is the gap that let this sit: a value the code **stopped** exporting is invisible to a test that walks the code. | S1-AC | **`NETWORK_STACK.md` §4.5's bogon filter has no counterpart in the client, and the attack it names is live: a provider record can make this client dial its own LAN.** §4.5 rule 2 says to drop RFC 1918, RFC 6598, loopback, link-local, multicast, broadcast and reserved ranges from DHT-derived candidates, and gives the reason in terms — *“a record in the public DHT claiming a private address is either pollution or an attempt to make us scan our own LAN”*. **It was never built, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight.** Under Mainline the candidate was a `SocketAddrV4` that application code parsed, so the check had somewhere to live. Under Kademlia the addresses never reach application code at all: they travel inside the DHT messages, go straight into `libp2p-kad`'s routing table, and `DialOpts::peer_id(peer)` asks the swarm to use whatever is there. `run::run`'s provider handler sees a `HashSet<PeerId>` and nothing else. There is no point in the flow where §4.5 could be applied as written. **What it costs is bounded but not zero.** `DIALS_PER_CYCLE = 8` caps the fan-out, `PeerCondition::DisconnectedAndNotDialing` stops a retry storm, and a dial is one connection attempt rather than a scan — so this is a nuisance and a small reflection surface, not an amplifier. But a stranger can spend one provider record to make every client in the lobby knock on a chosen address on its own LAN, and the corpus says that should be refused. **And the obvious fix is the wrong one, which §4.5 itself already knew.** *“This filter is not the same as the publish filter of §5.6 and the two must never be merged”* — mDNS dials RFC 1918 addresses on the LAN deliberately, because two players behind one router is a case this project explicitly cares about. So a blanket refusal of private addresses breaks a supported case. What is needed is a filter that can tell a DHT-derived address from an mDNS-derived one, and `libp2p-kad` does not offer a hook that distinguishes them: the candidate would have to be refused at dial time by provenance the swarm does not record. That is a design question and not a patch. **The design exists, it was adversarially checked from two sides, and neither side broke it.** The provenance signal this row said the swarm does not record **is** recorded: `DialOpts::peer_id(p).build()` sets `extend_addresses_through_behaviour: true` (`libp2p-swarm-0.47.1/src/dial_opts.rs:220`) and every address-carrying builder sets it `false` (`:204`), including `From<Multiaddr>`, which is `unknown_peer_id().address(a).build()` (`:163-167`). `Swarm::dial` then appends what the behaviour returns **only** when that flag is true (`lib.rs:467-470`), and logs a discard otherwise. So a `handle_pending_outbound_connection` that filters what `ipfs_kad` hands back touches the DHT path — `run.rs`'s `DialOpts::peer_id(peer)` — and is **structurally unable** to reach the mDNS path, which dials `swarm.dial(addr)` with the address in the options. That is the property §4.5 demands and the reason its own text gives for not merging this with §5.6's publish filter: two players behind one router must still find each other on `192.168.x`. **Shape:** a newtype `NetworkBehaviour` wrapping each `kad::Behaviour` field, delegating every method and filtering one — about 120 lines, no new dependency, no protocol or wire change. `run::reachable` is already the predicate and is already applied at one narrower site (`run.rs:1885`). Have it count what it drops, because the number nobody has is how many bogons the real Amino DHT actually hands this client, and a filter that counts produces it as a byproduct. **Two cheaper routes were checked and neither works.** `kad::Config::set_kbucket_inserts(BucketInserts::Manual)` governs only whether a peer is added to the routing table **once already connected** (`behaviour.rs:132-149`); it does not gate the addresses a dial uses, so it cannot refuse a bogon. Reading the addresses out of `Behaviour::kbucket(peer)` (`behaviour.rs:714`, whose entries carry `Addresses`) and dialling with `.addresses(filtered)` would set `extend_addresses_through_behaviour: false` and discard the behaviour set entirely — one site, a dozen lines — **but it regresses the ordinary case**: a provider that is not yet in the routing table at the instant `FoundProviders` fires has no readable address, and dialling it with an empty list refuses a peer that is fine. The current code dials by peer id precisely because the addresses may not be readable yet. **Not written.** What is bounded here is a nuisance and one connection attempt per bogon per cycle, capped by `DIALS_PER_CYCLE = 8`; the two findings this pass fixed instead were a mechanism evicting healthy seats and a wire format no second implementation could read. **BUILT.** `Bogonless<B>` wraps each `kad::Behaviour` and filters `handle_pending_outbound_connection`, delegating every other method; `Deref`/`DerefMut` keep every existing `swarm.behaviour_mut().ipfs_kad.…` call site unchanged. **The predicate is deliberately not `run::reachable`.** That one asks *“could the rest of the internet dial this”* and answers **no** for `/dnsaddr/bootstrap.libp2p.io`, which has no IP at all — right where it is used, and wrong here, because using it would have cut names and the bootstrap shape out of the routing table. `not_a_bogon` refuses an address only when it **carries an IP and that IP is somebody's own network**, and keeps anything it cannot judge: a filter that guesses is worse than one that admits what it does not know. RFC 6598 is spelled out because `Ipv4Addr::is_private` does not cover it, and the IPv6 masks are spelled out because `is_unique_local` is unstable. **It counts what it drops**, on the status line and only when the number moves, so *how many private addresses the real Amino DHT hands this client* — the figure nobody had — arrives as a byproduct of the defence rather than needing a second measurement. **AND THE NUMBER IS NOT SMALL.** This row estimated the cost as *“a nuisance and one connection attempt per bogon per cycle”*. Measured, ten seats, seven minutes, with no build competing for the machine: **every node refused between 2 493 and 5 798 private addresses**, median about 3 200 — n0 3 159, n1 2 935, n2 3 682, n3 2 643, n4 3 731, n5 3 195, n6 5 798, n7 2 586, n8 2 493, n9 3 940. The climb is steady rather than bursty: one node was at 771 by its 33rd second and 1 301 by its 93rd. So the public Amino DHT hands this client something like a thousand private addresses a minute, and before 2026-09-02 every one of them entered the dial candidate set. **Stated as an upper bound, because the filter cannot see the one thing that would make it exact.** `handle_pending_outbound_connection` is called on **every** outbound dial, not only DHT-derived ones, and the addresses a behaviour returns are appended only when `extend_addresses_through_behaviour` is true — which the behaviour is not told. So some of those 1 301 would have been discarded by the swarm anyway. What is certain is that `libp2p-kad`'s routing table held that many private addresses to offer, which is the same finding either way: the pollution §4.5 describes is real, continuous, and at a scale nobody had guessed. | FIXED: `src/net/swarm.rs` `Bogonless`, `not_a_bogon`; `src/net/run.rs`; `docs/NETWORK_STACK.md` §4.5 — **closed, and the missing figure measured** |

What is claimed is only that §4.4's sentence and §4.3's field are inconsistent, that the inconsistency is invisible today because the beacon does not exist, and that **the moment the beacon is built the two rules collide** — so whoever writes the missing `seed → button` paragraph (`S1-B`) has to answer the seating half in the same breath or the collision lands in code. | OWNER: `docs/PROTOCOL.md` §4.3 `n(4)` against §4.4; `src/table/join.rs` — **open, and it is the owner's; it must be answered together with `S1-B`** |

An ordinary lossless message that is the one being **awaited** — `message_id == received_message_id + 1` — **never touches `recv_array` at all** (`group_connection.c:498-500`): it is handed straight to the handler. Seat 9 was untouched because by then the snapshot was the whole table, and the early joiners recovered because a higher serial still followed. **And it has a clean control.** The run was repeated on the *same binary*, unchanged, and that time no accept landed late: all ten seats sealed, every roster stayed at ten — and the table played **41 hands, 40 finished**, against 15 in the run with two clobbered peers. Until it does, the two rosters can only be ranked by a proxy, never compared. | FIXED: `src/net/formation.rs` (`on_join_answer`), `src/net/joinwire.rs` (`JoinAcceptBody`, open) |

The send path is UDP-only to `gconn->addr.ip_port` while the peer counts as *direct*, and `gcc_conn_is_direct` is decided by the **inbound** direction alone: n5 kept hearing n0, so n5 kept sending to whatever address it held for n0, `sendto` reported success, and n5 had *“no TCP relays to fall back on”* (its own line at 158 s). **The address it held was replaceable by any ping.** `handle_gc_ping` stores a carried address via `gcc_set_ip_port` **unconditionally and silently** — over an address it is receiving from at that moment — and what a ping carries is `chat->self_ip_port`, which `ipport_self_copy` builds by **preferring a non-LAN echo** from the DHT: behind a NAT that is the router's WAN address. Offered to a peer on the same LAN it is poison; the router does not hairpin. And the sixty-second interval meant to throttle those offers throttled nothing: `last_sent_ip_time` is written once, at peer creation, and never after a send, so past a peer's first minute **every** ping to a not-direct peer carried the address, every twelve seconds. **The recovery is the 58-second peer timeout — logged on n5, inferred on n0.** n5 logs *“Send array stuck; timing out peer”* at 284.6 s, which is 226.8 + `GC_CONFIRMED_PEER_TIMEOUT`; n0's own `peer_timed_out` for n5 would fall at about the same second and **logs nothing**, and neither node logs a handshake between 284 and 330 s. The request that carried traffic was **n0's**: n0's `peer_timed_out` — silent, and tripped after 58 s without any of n5's pings or acks, since the peer-timeout clock is refreshed by lossy packets and fragments and never by an in-order lossless message — put n5 on n0's list, n0 sent a handshake request to n5's still-good address, and at n5 `handle_gc_handshake_request` **overwrote n5's stale address for n0 with the packet's real source** and reset the ids. Whether n5 had already dropped n0 decided only whether it saw that request as a new peer or logged *re-handshaking* (it logged neither, so it had). A first reading of this row said today's recovery was gentler than the earlier ones because n0's log had no timeout line; the line is the **sender's**, and it was on n5. **It is not new and it is not rare.** Counting one id re-sent ten or more times as a stall: ten of fourteen runs today had them, one to fifteen a run, and every run with a stall had a peer timeout. The founder's log alone shows five and six stalls in the 11:05 and 12:19 runs, each lasting 54 to 57 seconds. `S1-BK` cut the certificates this causes from 1.52 to 0.33 a run by making the *repair* fast; it could not touch a message that never reaches the socket. **The earlier design panel found this mechanism and this row set it aside.** Its address lens reported, verbatim, *“the address that makes a cross-subnet peer look ‘direct’ is the router's own WAN address, taken from the peer's PING and never validated or cleared”* — and `S1-BK`'s investigation filed it under *not the shape*, because the peers it was then looking at had clean carriers. They did; the carrier is clean in this failure too. For the first fourteen seconds of the fifty-six the mechanism is forbidden by the code it depends on. **So: the two defects are real, `patches/0012` is a guard for a real hazard, and 0012 is not the fix for this run's loss.** What the logs establish is narrower: n5→n0 UDP delivery died between 20:34:41.6 and 20:34:42.8 while n0→n5 stayed alive for the whole window. The cause is **not identified**. Candidates that fit a silent one-way UDP loss between two processes on one Windows host, all open: n0's UDP receive buffer overflowing under eight local instances plus DHT traffic; NAT or firewall connection state; an address change through the handshake path. **The instrument is also weaker than this row first claimed.** Hunk A's refusal line cannot fire within 16 s of a direct packet, so for a fault of this shape it counts nothing. What would decide it next run is two DEBUG lines that do not exist yet: the source `IP:Port` of every UDP packet handled for a peer, compared against `gconn->addr.ip_port`; and every change of a peer's stored address, with old value, new value and caller. That is `patches/0013`, and the refuters extended the list: every change of a stored address with old, new and caller; every packet handled for a peer whose source differs from the address held; each flip of a connection between *direct* and *relayed* and the first blind re-send of a stuck head, with destination and path; transitions of `self_udp_status` and `self_ip_port`; and the two receive-side early returns the enumeration found to be silent. All at DEBUG. Instrumentation, not a fix — and the first run that shows any of them at the moment a pair goes dark is the run that decides this row. **First run with `patches/0013` in, `split235537-9`, 420 s, nine seats:** packets arriving from an address other than the one held **0**, stored-address changes by ping or handshake **4**, direct/relayed flips **64** (one per peer at start is the baseline), first blind re-sends of a stuck head **147**, self-status or self-address changes **11**; stalls **0**, peer timeouts **0**, seats certified **0**, hands **15**. **What those lines said.** The poison happened, live, and to the far seat: at 96 s `far-n0` logged three times *“ping changed a peer's address from 192.168.1.20:3344x to 198.51.100.17:3344x”* — the local LAN's public IP, carried by the pings of three local seats — and `patches/0012`'s refusal line appears **zero** times in nine logs. It could not fire: it refuses only while the peer was heard directly within `GCC_UDP_DIRECT_TIMEOUT` (16 s), and a peer that has been quiet for 16 s is exactly the peer whose address the next ping overwrites. The guard stood aside in the one state that matters. Two more things the instrument showed. Every local node's DHT self-image is the public IP (`… -> 198.51.100.17:port` on all eight), because `ipport_self_copy` prefers the non-LAN echo, so every local ping to a not-direct peer offers the WAN address; hunk B withholds it only when the receiver is held at a LAN address, and on three seats `far-n0` evidently was not. And `far-n0` holds five of the eight local seats at **`172.16.0.1:port` — the far router**, not at 192.168.1.20: the two subnets NAT each other, and all seventy of `far-n0`'s blind re-sends went to those router addresses and were acked in the end. A peer we hold on our own LAN cannot be better reached through the public internet, whatever its ping says; the 0012 rule stays behind it for the direct case. The sender now also logs *“offered self address … to a peer held at …”*, so the next run shows both halves of an offer. | S1-BO | **FIXED by `patch 0015`, and it was never as latent as this row said: 44 of the 63 peer timeouts in the day's two bad runs follow a re-handshake on the same node.** An in-place re-handshake resets both message-id counters and the shared key and leaves both rings untouched, so it strands an old-numbered in-flight message, can deliver a stale one under a reused id, and refuses a new one whose slot is still occupied. Found by `S1-BN`'s handshake lens, read line by line and upheld by its refuter, and excluded for `S1-BN` itself on one fact that was true of the nine logs read that day and false of the next two runs: the branch logs *"Handshaked peer ... sent a handshake request; re-handshaking"* unconditionally at DEBUG, and that line appeared in none of those nine. **The lesson is the exclusion, not the mechanism.** This row named its own trigger line and then filed itself as not-firing on the strength of nine logs; two runs later the line was in every one of them. A latent row is only as latent as the last log searched. **The path.** A confirmed peer never re-handshakes on its own — `do_handshakes` skips a handshaked peer — so the trigger is always the *remote* having deleted us and re-added us as a new peer: `do_timed_out_reconn` (private groups, first try at the next 2 s tick, then every 36 s), a sync announce, `load_gc_peers`, or a DHT announce. On the side that receives the request, `handle_gc_handshake_request` recomputes the shared key from the peer's new session key, sets `received_message_id := 1`, and the response sets `send_message_id := 3` (and `send_array_start` with it); the requester's side goes to 2. **Nothing there touches `send_array` or `recv_array`** — the only clearers are `clear_array_entry`, `clear_send_queue_id_range` and `gcc_peer_cleanup` — and `confirmed` stays true, so the application sees neither an exit nor a join. **What that can do.** An in-flight message under the old numbering keeps its slot and its old id in the sender's ring; the resend walk starts from the new counter's slot, so the old entry is not re-sent until the new counter has passed it, and when it is, the receiver — whose expectation was reset small — stores it as far-future or, once the new counter reaches `old_id − 1`, **delivers the stale message as the new stream's next one**. New sends whose `id % 2048` lands on an occupied old slot are refused (`patches/0007`'s *“Failed to create send array entry”*). Packets sealed under the old key that arrive after the swap fail to unwrap, at DEBUG. A `GR_ACK_REQ` for an old id still finds it and re-sends it under the old id. **Measured, 2026-09-05.** The trigger line fires in `split115952-10` on `far-n0` 13 times, `far-n1` 6, `n1` 2, `n2` 1 and `n4` 2 - exactly the five nodes with *Send array stuck* (10, 5, 2, 1 and 2) and no other node; in `split121953-10` on all ten nodes, which is where all ten had timeouts; and in the clean `split094546-10` not once, alongside zero timeouts and zero send-array refusals on every node. **How much of the damage is this row, counted rather than asserted.** Of the 63 timeouts, 44 have a re-handshake before them on the same node and 24 of those are inside one 58-second window of it (median gap 57.6 s in `split115952-10`, 75.6 s in `split121953-10`); the remaining 19 have no re-handshake before them at all, they are the two early bursts between 171 and 192 s, and they stay with `S1-BN`. A gap wider than one window is still this mechanism and not a coincidence - a stale entry only becomes a timeout when the reset counter reaches the slot it sits in - but the honest claim is the correlation, not the arithmetic: the five nodes with the line are the five nodes with the timeout, ten of ten in the second run, and none of ten in the clean one. Clearing the ring removes a lie, not a safeguard; the bit is re-derived from live traffic on the two-second nudge tick, so a peer with anything genuinely in flight sets it again at once. | S1-BT | **OPEN: at a cryptographic stage the vote on a silent seat and this client's own abort fire in the same stall tick, at twice the budget — so a seat the carrier counts as mid-delivery can never be certified there, and a table that lost one seat's `HAND_INIT` loses every hand at 60 s and keeps the seat in R.** Read by the `S1-BS` panel and confirmed in `split092359-10`: the eight's hand #8 waited for seat 3 at stage 0; `vote_on_timeouts` holds the vote while the mid-delivery bit is set until `long_past_stage` (twice `crypto_step_timeout_ms`, 60 s), and `may_abandon` waits for the same instant when a certificate is possible; the stall tick runs the vote first and the abort next, so every voter casts its vote at its own 60 s and aborts in the same tick, the vote is `1/7` on every node (`n0` at 07:32:52 and again on hands #9 to #14), no certificate forms, and `took_part` keeps seat 3 in R for every hand after. Both sides move together and that is the point: the emitter's gate is `may_abandon` and the receiver's is the cause-1 admission, and if only one waited the first seat to reach its own bound would still end the hand everywhere. The receiver's gate also stops asking *has this client voted* and starts asking *is this client needed*: `party_to_vote` replaces `vote_joined`, because a seat whose own timer has not fired yet is still one of the voters the round needs, and under the old test that seat admitted a peer's abort at one budget and killed the round for the seats that had voted. **The bound.** At a cryptographic stage with a certificate possible, this client's own abort now fires at max(2x, own vote + 1x) and never later than 3x, where x is **the stage's own deadline** and not a constant - three budgets of a 30-second cryptographic stage is 90 s, three of a settling stage is three of whatever that stage budgets. Where no certificate is possible nothing moves: the emitter still gives the hand up at **one** budget, which is what `may_abandon` has always done once `past_deadline` passes and `certificate_possible` is false, and the receiver still admits a peer's abort at two, which is the bound `a_held_abort_is_admitted_at_twice_the_budget_without_a_certificate` pins. Betting stages and the whole-hand budget are untouched. **What it costs an honest table:** nothing on a hand with no stall, nothing on a dead seat whose mid-delivery bit is clear (the certificate completes around one budget, well before two), 62 to 72 s instead of a hand lost at 60 s when the bit is set - and the seat leaves R(k+2) instead of every later hand dying the same way - and 90 s instead of 60 s in the worst case, a round that is held and cannot complete. **D-026, stated exactly, because the first draft of this row was too comfortable.** No new way to end a hand is created, and at a cryptographic stage the abort refunds the start-of-hand stacks whichever way it fires, so no chip moves that did not move before. The honest slow seat keeps the full two-budget reprieve **from the abort**. What it does not keep is the reprieve from *removal*, and that is a real change: `S1-BK`'s lever suppresses a vote about a seat the carrier is still delivering only until twice the budget, *whatever the carrier says*, and until now that bound was inert because the abort killed every round before it could gather. Making the round complete makes the bound live, so a seat whose traffic is genuinely still in flight at two budgets now leaves `R(k+1)` where before it kept its place by accident. | S1-CA | **FIXED: a join needs two things at once - an advert and a dialable founder - and only the first was ever a trigger, so a client held a valid ticket for a minute at a time and never presented it.** The headless driver asks for a seat when a `TableSeen` event arrives, and that event is emitted only for an advert that gets past the limiter. `Window::admit` is a **tumbling** sixty-second window admitting four adverts per table key, while a founder publishes about ten a minute - a 30 s housekeeping re-advertise plus a re-signed shout to every new lobby subscriber, one per three seconds. So a joiner spends its whole minute in the first eight to ten seconds and is deaf for the rest: `RateLimited` becomes `TableRefused` and no `TableSeen` is emitted **even for a table the store still holds**. Every join failure meanwhile tears the state down (`table = None`, the carrier cleared, the topic unsubscribed), so the client is wholly dependent on that event. **Measured, and reproduced by two readers independently:** holes of 51.1 s (`split111249-10` `n3`, 77.1 to 128.2), 56.5 s (`split083343-9` `far-n0`, 26.2 to 82.7) and twice in one run, 49.9 s and 52.2 s (`split214929-9` `n7`, which was that run's slowest seat). In each of them the founder came up inside the hole and was not asked - `far-n0` logged it at 63.1 s, its next accepted advert at 82.7 s and its seat at **82.9 s**: nineteen and a half seconds holding a ticket it could not present. **The fix is the second edge**, the founder becoming dialable, with a five-second floor and a ceiling of eight asks per run, both in a pure function with a test; the advert edge is untouched and stays unbounded, so nothing that fires today stops firing. **Not a timer, deliberately:** a timer fires while the founder is undialable, which is exactly when the ask is futile - `n7`'s four asks inside one window were each answered *"the founder did not answer"* within a tenth of a second - whereas every seating in the corpus follows its ask by 0.1 to 0.5 s, so the edge fires only where the ask is about to succeed. **One defect in the first shape, found by a refuter.** The five-second floor was armed by an ask from **either** edge, and an advert-edge ask is often dropped before it leaves: the join request is discarded within the same poll when the swarm holds no address for the founder, which is the ordinary case the advert itself creates, and the very same command fires the query that makes the founder dialable a second or two later. So an advert ask armed the floor and silenced the founder edge in exactly the fast case the edge exists for. The floor is the founder edge's own now. **A second defect, from the next reader: the edge fired on the connection the join request itself had dialled.** The node refuses a `JoinTable` while one is in flight, so that ask was spent on nothing at the exact moment the driver was closest to a seat - and 21 of 524 joiner logs record the founder's connection dying with a request in flight, after which the founder stays connected and no further connection event is ever raised for it, which is this row's own hole reintroduced one level down. The driver now tracks its own join, and it is a **window rather than a latch** - the third shape, after I read the node's handler back and found three arms that answer with a `Warning` and `continue` and send no event at all: the table has left the node's own lobby store, the advert's founder id will not parse, the RNG failed. A flag those never clear would silence the founder edge for the life of the process, which is this row's own fault one level down. So an ask is **stamped**, `Seated`, `LeftTable` and `JoinRefused` clear the stamp, and the stamp lapses on its own after `JOIN_RPC_TIMEOUT_MS` + `REASK_FLOOR` = 35 s - the join RPC's own request timeout, past which the node itself calls the request failed, plus the margin between the timeout firing and `LeftTable` arriving. Overrunning it costs one ask answered with a warning, which is what the driver did before this row existed. Both edges of the window are tested. **One limit recorded rather than fixed.** `NodeEvent::PeerConnected` is advisory (`src/net/node.rs:368`), so `Events::send` offers it with `try_send` and drops it when the channel is full rather than waiting - deliberately, because a non-advisory send on a full channel stalls the whole `select!`. The founder edge is therefore a **one-shot trigger on a droppable event**: lose that one event and the driver is back to waiting for an advert. It is left as it is on evidence, not on argument - the node counts every drop and says so, and **none of the 644 logs on disk contains the line**. If one ever does, the answer is not to make the event reliable but to re-derive the condition from state the driver already holds, which is what the ask ceiling and the floor exist to bound. **Two things the readers corrected and the row keeps:** the hole explains the extreme tail rather than the whole bimodality (a run whose adverts were never rate-limited can still take a minute, for `S1-CB`'s reason), and most of the asks the hole delays would have failed anyway on the founder's dial - so this amplifies `S1-CB` rather than standing alone. **The two were meant to land together and did not**: `S1-CB`'s first design was refuted and reverted, so this one lands by itself and must not be expected to move the distribution on its own - the ask it saves still has to survive a dial priced at the full cycle. It is the **headless driver only**: the window a human clicks in is drawn from the store, which outlives the limiter's dead minute. **The run, `split122959-9`, 8+1, 420 s, no fault knobs, and the edge fired twice.** `n6` asked at 59.8 s and `n4` at 61.9 s, and each was **seated 0.1 s and 0.3 s later** - the bottom of the 0.1 to 0.5 s this row's own *not-a-timer* argument was built on, which is the argument checking out. Both had just made an advert-edge ask and lost it: the line immediately above each is *"the founder did not answer: Failed to dial the requested peer"*, which is the dropped-before-it-leaves case the first defect above is about, caught in a run rather than argued from the library. Without this edge both would have waited for the next advert the limiter admitted. | S1-CB | **BUILT at the third attempt, measured: a lobby provider whose dial failed waits a whole discovery cycle before it may be tried again, and for the first minute of a run that is the wrong price - the joiner is not waiting for want of information.** `REDIAL_AFTER` is sixty seconds and equals the crawl period, which is right for a record that may simply be dead. But a dial of a **live** peer fails for two reasons that both mend themselves in seconds: the DHT still serves the founder's **previous run's** circuit addresses, because seat identities are stable across runs and the founder's own announcement walk takes about twenty seconds; and the circuit hop collides, because `libp2p-relay` dials the relay with the default `DisconnectedAndNotDialing` condition and drops the pending circuit on **any** dial failure, so a circuit through a relay this client is already dialling dies synchronously as *"oneshot canceled"* - and twenty seconds later that relay is connected and the same address needs no dial at all. **Measured over the 34 split runs on disk, re-derived rather than taken:** seating time splits cleanly on whether every seat reached the founder inside thirty seconds - fifteen runs seat their last seat between 8 and 31 s, the other nineteen between 33 and 210 s, and **nothing lands in between** - with the slow tail clustering on the sixty-second quantum and its multiples. And the joiners hold the information the whole time: a joiner whose first dial missed then saw the founder in later answers a **median of 23 more times**, at most 78, while the cooldown refused to act on any of them. **A fix was built and reverted the same night, and the reversal is the useful half of this row.** It priced the cooldown on reported failures - ten seconds, five times, then the full cycle - and refuters took it apart on four grounds, two of which made it net harmful and one of which was a flooding vector the fix itself introduced. **(1) `DialError::Denied` reached the counter.** The arm above it swallows `Denied` only while the connection budget is below its ceiling, and **637 of the 644 logs on disk reach that ceiling**, at a median of 24.4 s, and 634 of them inside the first 120 s - inside the very window this row is about. `Denied` also has an asynchronous form, raised when a behaviour of **this** process refuses a connection that is already established - this client's own limiter - so the peer is provably alive, and the change charged it for our refusal, re-dialled it six times as often at the moment we were saturated, and then demoted it, the founder among them, for the life of the process. **(2) The counter was charged for dials this site never made:** the join request-response, `dcutr`, `autonat`, both `kad` behaviours and mDNS all dial these peers by id, and dcutr alone spends three dials per `AttemptsExceeded` - one log has 33 of those, about 99 charged failures for peers we hold a circuit to. So the lane silently stopped applying to the relayed and NATed seats that need it most. **(3) The eviction rule the fix introduced is a flooding vector.** Keeping the newest stamps evicts exactly the **demoted** providers, because the fast lane is what keeps a stamp fresh - and each returns with five fast dials again. Provider records are unauthenticated and peer ids are free, so a peer can fill the map with fakes, earn five fast dials per fake, and renew them on every eviction cycle: past the cap the client sits pinned at the redial ceiling instead of decaying, and never recovers. **(4) The evidence offered for that eviction rule was the wrong quantity.** The 598 and 590 counted providers **offered** - `NodeEvent::LobbyPeer` is sent before every filter and before the insert - not providers **dialled**. Replaying the loop the way the code walks it gives a map peak of **346** across the 601 logs the corpus held when it was replayed, against a cap of 512; the old comment's *peak 318* reproduces exactly at `split215815-2/far-n0`, so the sentence being replaced was measuring the right thing. Crossing 512 needs **both** a lobby that offers more than 512 distinct providers **and** ten to twelve minutes of uptime, and no run on disk has both: the 15-minute runs peak at 104-268 because their lobbies are small, and the 600-provider lobbies were observed for 262-400 s. The eviction is therefore unreachable in the corpus - the hazard in (3) has to be forced - and the honest argument for the rule was always the correctness one, never an observed fault. That is a claim this row made after grepping for a number without checking that the grep counted the right thing. **What the refutation points at, and what should be built instead:** the fast lane belongs to **the founder of a held advert**, not to every lobby provider. That is a set of size one rather than 346. It cannot be forced by fake ids, because a fake is not the founder named in an advert this client holds; it makes the eviction question vanish, because one entry is not evicted; and it shrinks (2) rather than dodging it - the join RPC dials the founder by the same behaviour-supplied addresses the crawl uses, so a failure there is the same fact about the same peer, and only `dcutr` and `autonat` remain to be excluded by connection id; and it is the only peer the measurement was ever about. The general fast lane was a bigger mechanism than the fault. **And that design is wrong too, which `split122959-9` showed the same night it was written.** The run timed four things for every seat - when the founder was first **offered** in a lobby answer, when it was first **identified** as a poker peer, when the **advert** arrived, and when the seat sat down. The four fast seats: `n1` 0.6 / 1.2 / 5.1 / 6.2, `n3` ~1 / 2.3 / 3.9 / 5.0, `n5` ~1 / 1.2 / 2.6 / 3.7, `far-n0` 1.7 / 2.2 / 2.3 / 3.5. The four slow ones: `n4` **1.9 / 62.0** / 60.5 / 62.2, `n2` **2.7 / 62.6** / 63.5 / 65.3, `n7` **11.9 / 57.4** / 57.5 / 58.3, `n6` **12.7 / 59.8** / 59.0 / 59.9. Every seat had the founder in a lobby answer inside thirteen seconds; four of them then took **forty-five to sixty more** to connect to it, and each of those was seated 0.3 to 2.7 s after connecting. The gap is one `REDIAL_AFTER`, sitting exactly where this row says it does, and it is now measured per seat rather than inferred from a distribution. **And the joiner held the founder the whole time, counted:** the founder was offered again in a later lobby answer **20, 31, 24 and 27 times** before each of `n4`, `n2`, `n6` and `n7` connected to it, and the cooldown refused every one. Those are not repeats of one record - each is a fresh answer, dialled through whatever addresses `kad` holds at that moment, which is a different attempt each time. **One caveat this row owes itself:** `REDIAL_AFTER` is 60 s and `discover_timer` is 60 s, so *the cooldown refused* and *the next crawl had not yet brought a usable address* are indistinguishable in any run taken with the two equal - all four seats connect at 57-63 s regardless of whether they first saw the founder at 1.9 s or at 12.7 s, which fits the crawl period at least as well as it fits a per-seat cooldown started at discovery. Under `D-019` a hand event is a lossless group packet, and toxcore's ring never loses one inside `GC_CONFIRMED_PEER_TIMEOUT` = 58 s: `gcc_resend_packets` (`group_connection.c:715`) re-sends an unacked entry at 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 s from `time_added`, the receiver asks for the head of any gap with `GR_ACK_REQ` (`group_chats.c:6454`, `:6468`), `handle_gc_message_ack` answers with an immediate re-send, and only a head entry 58 s old times the peer out (`:727`). So a seat whose line is cut for less than that receives every frame it missed, late and in order, as soon as the line returns. The knob's receive side — the Tox path's `if link_is_down() { continue; }` and the two GossipSub sites — steps past a frame the ring has **already delivered and acked**, so the frame is gone for good; its send side is closer to the real thing, because `publish_hand` parks what could not leave in `said` and the re-send arm puts it out once `nothing_leaves()` is false. **What the knob models is a peer whose transport forgets what it received while the line was down — GossipSub's semantics, which has no history — and not the group's.** Verified in `split123139-9`: after its 40-second window the seat received `List(NotNewer { got: 8, held: 8 })` re-broadcasts, 107 of them to the end of the run, and not one frame of the hand it was in; the ring had delivered those into the discard thirty seconds earlier. **Consequences.** Every `-LinkDown` run in the corpus measured a permanent loss and not an outage — `split220636-9` among them, one of `S1-BW`'s two failed reproductions — and the case the owner put in scope when `S1-Q` was closed (*“stačí ošetřit krátkodobé výpadky internetu”*: a seated player whose link drops for seconds and returns) **has still never been measured**; the doc's own sentence that *did the hand recover* *“has never had one [an instrument]”* stayed true after the knob was built for it. **The honest instrument for the downlink already exists and was labelled as idle.** Patch 0016's `-Deaf` drops a group packet before the ring sees it (`group_chats.c:6369`, above `group_packet_unwrap` and `gcc_handle_received_message`), so the senders keep re-sending and the seat receives everything at the window's end; the harness said *“-DeafFor must exceed 58 s or nothing is timed out and the knob does nothing at all”*, which is exactly wrong under 58 s — there it is the brief-outage model, and over 58 s it is patch 0015's re-handshake model. | S1-CO | **A seat that misses N lossless messages gets them back one per second, because the receiver asks for one id per request, at most one request per second, and only when a later packet happens to arrive — so a 20-second downlink outage costs the seat about 32 seconds and its place at the table.** The first brief-outage measurement (`S1-CM`, `split162916-9`, `-DeafSeat 3 -DeafAt 240 -DeafFor 20`, node `n3` = seat 5) refuted every clause of its booked prediction: seat 5 missed the shuffles of seats 1–3 sent at 320.3 s, received the first of them at 352.3 s — twelve seconds after its window closed at 340.4 — while the peers' 30 s clock on seat 5 ran out at 349.6 s (`n7`: *“I am at stage 12, 5 last heard at stage 1”*), certified it out at 350.0–358.3 s and voided the hand; 16 hands against 20. A fragmented message is worse, because `handle_gc_packet_fragment` refuses an out-of-order chunk and stores nothing (`:6241`), so a shuffle of several 500-byte chunks (`MAX_GC_PACKET_CHUNK_SIZE`) comes back chunk by chunk at that rate; and the sender's blind schedule (2, 4, 8, 16, 32 s from `time_added`, `gcc_resend_packets`) has nothing between 16 and 32. **Two forms of the fix, the first refuted by measurement before the second was built.** The first form of patch 0024 was a silence probe: after two seconds without a processed packet the receiver asks the peer for its head. Prediction booked in the patch header: first missed frame within three seconds of the window's end, no certificate, no abort. `split164858-9` (same recipe, `n3` = seat 8): the probe fired — 292 lines at `n3`, and `n7` answered *“Re-sent requested packet 2455”* every two seconds through the window, each answer dropped as designed — and the seat still got seat 7's shuffle 12.9 s after the window (14:55:17.3 against 14:55:04.4), `n7` answering 2456, 2457, 2458, 2459, 2460 at 04.9, 06.6, 08.9, 10.6, 13.6; certified out at 351.5–356.8, abort at 359.5, 18 hands against 23. The probe moved the first request earlier and could not move the rate, which the refuted prediction says plainly; its header had also named the wrong falsifier (*“if the frame still arrives at +32 s”* — +32 was never the mechanism), and the patch record says so. **The second form is a burst.** Once a second per handshaked peer, `p2p_poker_ask_for_what_is_missing` (`group_chats.c`, above `do_peer_connections`) asks for every id from the head of the gap to the highest id the peer has ever shown this node — a new `p2p_poker_highest_seen`, written at unwrap before the fragment path can refuse and forget — sixteen at a time, skipping ids already buffered; a peer that has shown nothing but has been quiet two seconds is asked for its head alone. Each request is the standard `GR_ACK_REQ` that `handle_gc_message_ack` answers only when it holds the id, so an unpatched peer on the public network sees nine-byte packets it either answers or ignores, and compatibility is kept. Marker 35 in `tools/build-tox.ps1`, broken and restored. **The prediction for the burst run is booked before it is taken**, same recipe: the first missed frame arrives within three seconds of the window's end; the sender's log shows consecutive ids re-sent within one second right after it; no certificate about `n3`, no abort, `n3` finishes as many hands as the others. The falsifier is the drain still taking ten seconds or more — which would mean the bottleneck is not the request side, and the next place to look is the sender's answer path. **Confirmed, every clause, 2026-09-10, `split120908-9`.** The window fell into hand 16's shuffle round: `n3` (seat 8 this time, the last shuffler) had seats 0–4 by 290.9 s and then nothing; its first burst after the window went out at 311.6 s (*“asking peer 1 for messages 2691..2706 (16 sent, highest seen 2879)”*), the senders answered in bursts at one offset — `far-n0` 2306..2317, `n0` 2778..2788, `n1` 2163..2174, consecutive ids in the same second — and `n3` sealed the deck at 313.0 s, under two seconds after the window's end. The peers had waited for seat 8 about 21 s, inside the 30 s clock: no tally, no certificate, no abort anywhere in the run, and every one of the nine seats opened 22 hands and finished 21. The same outage that cost a seat its place in two runs cost it nothing in the third. `tools/read-deaf-run.py` reads a `-Deaf` run this way — the window, the first frame after it, every certificate, and each sender's answers at their offsets, so a drain and a burst look different on the page; its window arithmetic is approximate because the C anchors on the first group packet handled, which preceded the join line by 4 s here. **What this does not settle**: the uplink half of an outage (`S1-CM`, a wire-level mute behind the ring) is still not built, so a symmetric outage has still not been measured; and the burst's cost on a lossy public link is bounded by construction and now has one reading, from the same run: a healthy seat logged 396–529 requests in 420 s (9–11 B/s of payload, peaks of 7–16 in a second) and the deaf seat 1 051, with a peak of **159 requests in the second its window closed** — eight peers asked for sixteen ids each plus the probes, the designed worst case; the quiet probes that go unlogged add at most one nine-byte packet per peer per two seconds on top. Whether it does is the whole question: after the window its downlink repairs in a second, and if the table is waiting on a frame that is *already stuck in its uplink* — its shuffle, its action — it has nothing new to send, and a multi-chunk shuffle drains for eight to twenty seconds against a thirty-second clock that started inside the window. **Instrument, built** (patch 0025, fault harness only): `P2P_POKER_DEAF_UPLINK=1` beside the 0016 variables makes `gcc_send_packet` (`group_connection.c`) drop this node's own lossless and lossy group packets during the same window, *after* the ring took them, and report success as a cut wire does; handshakes pass, as 0016 lets them pass on the way in; the window and its anchor are 0016's, hoisted to file scope so both halves read one clock, and a send before the anchor exists is not muted, so the anchor is not moved by a send. `tools/table-run-split.ps1 -DeafBothWays`; the `deaf` header says which halves; marker 36, broken and restored. **The prediction is booked before the run**, `-DeafSeat 3 -DeafAt 240 -DeafFor 20 -DeafBothWays` on the 8+1 rig, and it splits on the one fact above: if the seat has something new to send right after the window, the peers see a newer id, burst the gap closed within a second, and the run shows no certificate and the seat level with the others; if the table is waiting on a frame stuck in the window, the peers' logs show *“Re-sent requested packet”* answered **by `n3`** one id every two seconds, the clock runs out, and `n3` is certified out — which would name the sender-side half of `S1-CO`'s defect. The second is the outcome to expect when the window lands on the seat's own shuffle, and the fix it would call for is already sketched: when a peer quiet for two seconds or more is heard again, the sender pushes everything that peer has not acked, sixteen at a time — zero cost at idle, because it fires only on a resumption. | S1-CQ | **A brief outage of one seat kills the far seat's paths to the rest of the table, because the local mesh's relays wake for the outage and go to sleep when it ends, and a relay going to sleep takes every out-of-band slot on it with it.** Measured twice on 2026-09-10 with the symmetric outage (`S1-CP`, 20 s, one local seat): in `split123725-9` `n3`'s connection to the far seat read *“0 online, 0 registered, 4 other, 6 slots”* from the second its window closed, 1 034 sends found no relay in the next minute, and the pair timed each other out; in `split125153-9` **six of eight local peers** lost the far seat at the same moment of `n3`'s window — `n0` 2 507 failed sends, `n6` 2 603, `n1` 2 199, `n2` 2 236, `n4` 2 167, `n7` 2 038, all timing it out at 332–339 s, the far seat timing six of them out at 334–347 — while `n3` and `n5` kept it. **What the code says.** A seat with no direct route lives on `REGISTERED` relay slots: the relay answered the routing request (`tcp_response_callback`, `TCP_connection.c:1283`), the peer is not routed but out-of-band delivery works, and such a slot **locks nothing** — only `ONLINE` slots `++lock_count` (`:1329`). `do_tcp_conns` (`:1877`) puts a relay to sleep when `lock_count > 0` and `lock_count == sleep_count`, i.e. when every connection-to that locks it is itself asleep; `do_gc_tcp` (`group_chats.c:7662`) sleeps a connection-to whenever its peer is direct and wakes it whenever it is not, every tick; and `sleep_tcp_relay_connection` (`:1130`) kills the TCP client and sets **every slot on that relay to `NONE`** (`:1179`) — the far seat's `REGISTERED` ones included, which then carry nothing (patch 0018's *other*). So the chain, as a hypothesis: the outage makes the deaf seat *not direct* for its neighbours at +16 s, their connection-to for it wake, their relays reconnect and register every connection-to on them, the neighbours and the deaf seat come `ONLINE` on those relays and lock them; the window ends, the seat is direct again, the connection-to sleep, the locks turn into sleepers, and ten seconds later the relays go to sleep with the far seat's out-of-band paths on board. Nothing wakes them for the far seat, because its connection-to is always awake and `set_tcp_connection_to_status(true)` on an awake one is a no-op (`:810`). In steady state the same relays carry the far seat because they hold no `ONLINE` route at all — `lock_count` 0 — and the sleep rule never fires; the outage is what puts a lock on them. **This is `S1-AA`'s family** — the reaper that takes `REGISTERED` slots was measured there (37 of 37) — and this is the first recipe that produces the loss on demand, twice in two runs. **Instrument, built** (patch 0026, marker 37, eight `LOGGER_DEBUG` lines, nothing changed in what is done): the relay sleep with the counts that decided it and what it takes (*“relay N goes to sleep (lock_count k == sleep_count k): … K registered, K of them out-of-band paths of an AWAKE connection-to”*), the wake, the connection-to sleep and wake, the routing response and both arms of the status callback. **The prediction is booked before the instrumented run**, same recipe: within a few seconds of the window's end the local peers' logs show *goes to sleep* lines whose *out-of-band paths of an AWAKE connection-to* count is at least one on the relays the far seat was registered on, no *wakes up* for those relays while the far seat lives, and the peers that lose the far seat are exactly the peers with such a line. The falsifier is the far seat dying at a peer with no sleep line at all — then the `NONE` writes come from the reconnect path (`:1075`) or somewhere unread, and this chain is wrong. **The fix, if the chain holds, is one clause**: a relay that carries a `REGISTERED` slot of an awake connection-to is in use and must not sleep — count such slots as locks in the sleep rule, or check for them in `sleep_tcp_relay_connection`. Local behaviour only, no wire change, compatible with the public network by construction. Not built until the instrument has read. **The instrument read (`split130548-9`, 2026-09-10), and the chain was right about the event and wrong about the slot.** At every local peer, in the second its connection-to for the deaf seat went back to sleep — *“connection-to 7 sleeps (peer direct)”* at `n0` 284.7 s, one node per 0.7 s from `n7` at 276.9 — its relays logged *“goes to sleep (lock_count 8 == sleep_count 8): 8 online slot(s), 0 registered, 0 of them out-of-band paths of an AWAKE connection-to”* and set every slot to `NONE`; `n0` then failed 3 602 sends to the far seat (*“0 online, 0 registered, 3 other”*) and timed it out at 342 s, `n1` 2 247, `n2` 2 557, `n3` 1 378, `n4` 2 620, `n5` 2 852, while `n6` and `n7` kept it — `n6` because its far slot sat on relay 10, which did not sleep. So the losing clause of the prediction is **refuted**: the far seat's slot at the five losers was `ONLINE`, not `REGISTERED`, its connection-to was awake (*“connection-to 0 is ONLINE on relay 0; lock_count 1, sleep_count 0”* at 258.0, never a sleep line for it), and the out-of-band count was zero; only `n3`'s relay 2 showed the out-of-band case (*“1 registered, 1 of them out-of-band paths of an AWAKE connection-to”*). **Which leaves the question the instrument was built to answer: how could `lock_count == sleep_count` hold with an awake peer `ONLINE` on the relay?** One function deeper. `sleep_count` is the number of `ONLINE` slots whose connection-to is asleep; going to sleep adds one per `ONLINE` slot (`set_tcp_connection_to_status`, the sleep branch), and **waking never takes them away** — the wake branch only sets `unsleep` on sleeping relays (`:809`–`:850`); the only other decrement is a peer leaving the relay (`tcp_status_callback`, status 1) or the connection-to being wiped (`:781`). Every sleep-wake-sleep cycle of a direct peer's connection-to therefore leaves one phantom sleeper on each relay it is `ONLINE` on, and an outage is exactly one such cycle at every neighbour: not direct at +16 s, direct again at the end. Eight peers `ONLINE`, seven asleep, one phantom — `lock 8 == sleep 8`, and the awake far seat's lock is covered. An upstream defect in `c-toxcore`, and the reason a healthy table never shows it is that a healthy table never cycles. **Fixed, in two parts (patch 0027, marker 38, broken and restored)**: (A) the wake branch decrements `sleep_count` for each `ONLINE` slot of the waking connection-to, the mirror of the sleep branch — with it a relay an awake peer is `ONLINE` on reads `lock > sleep` and stays awake; (B) a `REGISTERED` slot of an awake connection-to counts as a use in the sleep rule and in the reaper (`p2p_poker_relay_carries_awake_oob`, on 0026's counting helper), for `n3`'s case. Local behaviour only, nothing on the wire. **The prediction for the fixed run is booked before it is taken**, same recipe: at the window's end no relay at any local peer sleeps under an awake `ONLINE` slot — no *goes to sleep* line with `lock == sleep` in that minute — no *no relay carried* storm, nobody times the far seat out and it times nobody out, the hand the window fell into completes, every seat finishes level. The falsifier is a sleep line with `lock == sleep` at the window's end again, or the far seat lost by anyone. **Confirmed on every observable that matters, 2026-09-10, `split132427-9`, with one clause of the wording corrected.** Nobody lost the far seat: **zero** *no relay carried* at every local node in the minute after the window and at the far seat after 90 s, zero timeouts after the window anywhere (the far seat's six exit-type-1 deletions and `n4`'s one are all at 57–73 s — `S1-AA`'s join-phase shape, two hundred seconds before the window), zero certificates and zero aborts in the run, hand 11 — the one the window fell into — over at 298.8 s, and **every one of the nine seats opened 20 hands and finished 19**; the uplink burst worked as before (`n3` answered 1574..1589 in one second). Relays *did* still go to sleep at the window's end — nine lines across six nodes, `n4` *“relay 0 goes to sleep (lock_count 7 == sleep_count 7): 7 online slot(s)”* — and with (A) in place that equality means what it was always meant to mean: every connection-to `ONLINE` on the relay is asleep, no awake peer is on it, it may sleep; the far seat's slot was on none of them, which the zero failed sends prove. So *“no sleep line with `lock == sleep`”* was too strong a paraphrase; *“no relay sleeps under an awake `ONLINE` slot”* is the clause, and it held. Three symmetric runs before the fix lost the far seat three times; the one after it lost nothing. (A) is an upstream defect in `c-toxcore` 0.2.23's `set_tcp_connection_to_status` and is worth reporting there; the report is drafted in `docs/upstream/c-toxcore-tcp-connection-sleep-count.md` with the instrumented lines and the one-hunk fix, and **filed on the owner's word on 2026-09-10 as `TokTok/c-toxcore#3081`** (part A only, against `master`, which carries the same wake branch; from the `qavryxdev` fork, branch `fix/tcp-connection-sleep-count`). The vendored patch 0027 stays until a release carries the fix; on the next toxcore bump, check whether part A is upstream before re-applying it. | FIXED: `vendor/c-toxcore/toxcore/TCP_connection.c` (`p2p_poker_count_relay_users`, `sleep_tcp_relay_connection`, `unsleep_tcp_relay_connection`, `set_tcp_connection_to_status`, `tcp_response_callback`, `tcp_status_callback`), `patches/0026-every-relay-slot-transition-says-what-it-took.patch`, `patches/0027-a-waking-connection-to-takes-its-sleepers-back.patch`, `tools/build-tox.ps1` (markers 37, 38), `S1-AA`, `S1-CP`, `S1-Q` — **measured three times, lost three times; the instrument read the chain and refuted its losing clause; the root is a phantom sleeper an upstream wake path never returns; the two-part fix is built, gated and measured — the same outage that cost the far seat every time cost nothing, nine seats level** |
| S1-CR | **A client does not know after a restart that it left a session unfinished, and a client whose session is over must not keep trying to rejoin it.** Asked by the project owner on 2026-09-10 while `S1-BM` was being built. Today nothing about a session survives the process: no record of the table, the seat, the hand reached or the peers, so a restarted client opens the lobby as if nothing had happened, and a client that lost its table mid-hand has no rule for when to stop looking for it. **What to build.** A session record beside the profile -- `table_id`, `session_id`, `my_seat`, the founder's peer id, the last `hand_id` with its `TERMINAL(k)`, and the last contact time -- written at every boundary and deleted when the session ends (the tournament finished, or this seat left). On start, a record that is present means an unfinished session: the client tries to rejoin it before it does anything else, and **the window asks first** -- *an unfinished game at table X, seat N, stack S: rejoin?* -- while a headless client takes a switch. **When to stop.** The record is dropped when the rejoin finds the session finished, and the client gives up when the table's advertisement is gone AND no peer of the session has been reachable for about ten minutes; until then it keeps trying at the lobby's own cadence. The rejoin itself rides `S1-BM`: a seat that comes back outside the roster with chips asks at the next settled boundary and is dealt into the hand after. **Built 2026-09-10, tests first (D-029), and the rejoin needed one thing the register had not seen: a hand.** A restarted client re-entered the group before this (`S1-O` measured it), and then held nothing -- hand 1 from formation is the wrong hand, and there was no other. `Opening::adopt` takes the running hand from a strict majority of the members' own `HAND_INIT` copies at one genesis (the parent is the genesis, the body the stacks and positions, the signers the required set, the roster hash and the blind schedule checked), the decisive test follows an adopted hand as a bystander to the members' own checkpoint, and the node adopts every hand until D-028's return has dealt the seat back in. The record, the window's question, `--resume`, the give-up rule and the founder's refusal are as designed above. The first run of the rejoin (`run195623-3`) re-entered the group and sat at *ratified 1/3* for the rest of the run -- nobody sends a ratification again once the mesh's duplicate cache has refused the repeat and the group's copy went out before the seat was in it -- so a member whose table has dealt now answers a ratification copy arriving over the group with every one it holds (D-029 point 7). Two things kept that from running, both an intent recorded as a result. **(1)** The relay-circuit arm of `SwarmEvent::NewListenAddr` — where a client behind a NAT announces first, because its first external address is a circuit — still set the flag the moment `start_providing` returned `Ok` and never recorded the dispatch, so the tick's guard never let a re-walk through. **(2)** The confirmation, this client seeing its own `PeerId` among the lobby's providers, was answered by the client itself: `start_providing` stores the record in the local `MemoryStore` first, and `get_providers` reports that store as a `FoundProviders` before any request leaves, with `QueryStats::empty()` (`libp2p-kad-0.49.0/src/behaviour.rs:1024-1034, 1060-1105`); both arms issue that lookup in the same breath as the announcement, so every announcement was confirmed at once on either road. A node's answer carries the query's statistics, which count the request that reached it (`query.rs:397-403`, `behaviour.rs:2365-2398`); go-libp2p nodes return the asker its own record, rust-libp2p nodes filter it out (`behaviour.rs:1252`). **Measured before the fix**, `announce-before-121050` (one headless client, `--no-mdns`, the `c429e70` build, 482.7 s): the circuit at 4.4 s, *announced in the public lobby* once at 16.7 s, and no second walk in the 466 s after, though one was due from 304 s. **Fixed:** `run::LobbyAnnounce` holds the dispatch time, whether a walk has delivered, and the confirmation. Both arms walk when `due` — never walked, or 300 s since and still unconfirmed — and a dispatch records only its time. A walk that finishes `Ok` with successes counted has handed the record on (the nodes it reached are exactly the ones it sends to, `closest.rs:395-406`, `behaviour.rs:1557-1576`; a timed-out walk sends nothing, `:1730-1743`). A sighting confirms only from an answer a request was made for and only after delivery, said once as *public lobby: this client's own record came back from the network*. **Why delivery is required, measured:** `announce-after-122327` (latch fixed, sightings gated on requests only, 720 s, a fresh identity) confirmed at 33.6 s, half a second after the dispatch and twenty-two seconds before its walk had sent the record anywhere — three nodes named the new `PeerId` within two seconds, from a source neither library explains. **Measured with the fix** (instrumented, each run a fresh identity): `announce-probe-123805` walked at 4.0 s, ignored its own store's answer (no request), finished the walk at 15.0 s having reached 81 nodes, and was first returned the record by a node at 62.9 s; `announce-final-125214`, the committed rule, walked at 3.0 s, finished at 16.0 s (84 nodes reached), confirmed at 62.7 s on the first node's answer after its store's, and walked once in 422.7 s. `public lobby: nobody else yet` is now said of a lobby lookup that ends having found nobody but this client — it had been said at the end of any provider lookup, relay lookups included, while the flag was false, and only the vacuous confirmation kept it quiet; zero such lines in the final run, whose lookups all found players. It lacked ONE message every other seat had, so the table moved on and waited for it while it waited for the sender -- a split view, in all three runs. The carrier keeps a connection's messages in rings of 2048 slots, slot = id modulo 2048, and two things in it are upstream's: the periodic drain (`gcc_check_recv_array`) took whatever sat in the awaited message's SLOT for the awaited message and never compared the id; and a message stored out of order, whose retransmission then arrives in order before the drain has run, is handled straight away while its stored copy is never cleared. So a copy sat in its slot for a lap of the ring, and 2048 messages later the drain replayed it: handed it to the application again, acknowledged it under its OLD id, and moved the counter past a message that had not arrived -- which, when it came, was a duplicate by its number, dropped and acknowledged, so the sender forgot it too. **A lossless stream lost one message to one receiver with no error anywhere**, and this project's own repairs had made the race systematic: a receiver asks at once for what it misses (0009) and a sender answers with a run of consecutive ids (0024), which arrives in one batch and overtakes every copy stored ahead of it. **The sender's half was in the logs all along**, as upstream's own line *Wrap-around on message N*: 2, 109 and 205 of them in the three runs, N always small (123 to 776, the first lap), none in the first 250 s of any run and none before a counter had passed 2048, every one at a moment a receiver's counter passed N + 2048 (no other offset fits them all: + 1024 fits 0 to 12 per cent, + 4096 0 to 4), in runs of consecutive ids. Patch 0039 clears the copy with its message and makes the drain clear, never process, an occupant whose id is not the awaited one -- a leftover by construction, since a sender's own ring holds 2047 unacknowledged messages and no more; that also shuts out a member who sends awaited + 2048 on purpose. **Measured after**, the same rig the same evening, four runs (`split195458-9`, `split200404-9`, `split201156-9`, `split202100-9`): `REPLAYED` 0 in all four where the three before had 205, 109 and 2; the copy cleared with its message 4 475, 104, 8 and 556 times, which is how many leftovers a run had been making; the drain's own check never had to fire; and no clock ran out on any seat in any of them, with 13, 24, 28 and 23 hands opened. A seven-minute run only lets the leftovers of the first few hundred ids come round; at a table played for an hour all of them do. **The closing libp2p connections** are relayed ones ending at their relay's limit: every reservation in all three runs reported 131 072 bytes and 120 s (the client's own note says *NOT enough to carry a hand*), all 208 departures of `split185900-9` ended on a connection that was still relayed and not one on a connection DCUtR had made direct, lifetimes median 115 s, p90 120 s, 118 of 208 between 90 and 120 s; the bed runs with local discovery off, so eight clients behind one router meet through public relays and mostly cannot punch through to each other. The hand does not travel on those connections. **What re-opens it:** a `REPLAYED` or a `CLEARED` above zero from `tools/fold-ring-leftovers.py`, or a hand stalled with `REPLAYED` 0, which would be another cause. Before this verdict the cell read: OPEN: `src/tox/table.rs`, `src/net/run.rs`, `tools/table-run-split.ps1` -- **measured and not investigated**, filed so that the next reader of a run with *my clock has run out* in it counts hands and not lines. The instrument is in every log already: group the clock lines by hand and by the seat they name. What would move it: the same count over a campaign of plain runs at two times of day, which says whether it is the evening; and one run with the ninth seat held back until the table is set, which says whether it is the late entry. |

`Search::was_relayed` latches the first *behind NAT* for the length of a search, and **its own doc comment already said why**: *"Its own reading flaps — AutoNAT says reachable and behind NAT within a second"* — a witness written in the tree before this row was looked for, and a workaround for a cause nobody had found. The player's red *No way in from the internet* is shown only while no relay is held, so the flap was invisible where it looked worst. | FIXED: `src/net/run.rs` (`publicly_reachable`, `dialable_without_a_relay`, `relay_advert`, the AutoNAT arm), `src/net/node.rs` (`Reachability { public, ways_in, confirmed }`), `src/app/mod.rs` (the line carries both counts and reads nothing into them: under the control knob the verdict and the addresses disagree on purpose, and a line that explained the verdict would be the one thing in the log that lied), `tools/read-reachability.py`, `tools/table-run.ps1` (`-LastAddressVerdict`, in the run header), `NETWORK_STACK.md` §9.2, §9.6 — **the verdict is `swarm.external_addresses().any(dialable_without_a_relay)`, and a circuit is not one of them**; the relay advertisement follows it both ways now, which is safe only because the verdict is steady. `net::run::tests::the_reachability_verdict_is_read_from_every_confirmed_address` pins the case that was wrong and fails on both breaks — the circuit guard dropped, and the set not read at all; `the_relay_advertisement_follows_the_verdict_both_ways` pins the latch. **Control and treatment from one binary**, `P2P_POKER_LAST_ADDRESS_VERDICT=1` under fault-harness, four alternating runs of eight seats: the treatment wrote **nothing at all** -- 16 seat logs over two runs of 420 s, the verdict never leaving *behind NAT*, which is this machine's truth -- while the control, from the same binary in the same hour, wrote **46 turns in 14 of its 16 logs**, 14 of them within thirty seconds of the turn before and four under half a second, and **every one of its 26 *reachable from the internet* verdicts was taken with no way in confirmed**. The two arms played alike (29 to 33 hands a run, 11.3 to 11.4 s a hand) and reached the same relays (10 to 12 relay offers a run, 35 to 68 circuit addresses), so what differs between them is the rule and not the network.
