   table (§3.1), so a seat certified out is out of a hand, not of the table: removed from the group, not for
   good -- it is invited again when it returns (D-031). A seat the roster dropped is out for good.
2. **Every member acts on the word it verified itself.** `patches/0034` gives the library two local lists
   per chat, by group encryption key: keys the word removed for good (`peer_add` refuses them for the chat's
   life) and keys the founder may kick. On the word a member allows the kick, drops the seat's every entry
   from its own view of the group (the saved-peer entry goes with it, `patches/0031`), and, where it is the
   founder, kicks -- a kick every member honours because every member allowed it on the same word. A lingering member
   is gone from every view whether or not the founder lives.
3. **A founder's kick without the word is ignored** -- by every member, the target included -- and logged
   (*a kick without the table's word is ignored*). The founder that sends one changes nothing but its own
   view. The wire is untouched: no new packet, no new field; our groups are private and hold only our
   clients, and a client of the public network in a group of its own is unaffected.
4. **A member the word removed hears it** (the moderation event, `Event::GroupModeration`): it leaves the
   group it held, so an invitation can bring it back -- a group held refuses one -- and its window is told.
5. **Measured.** `run145130-3` (three seats, one killed at ~47 s mid-tournament): the survivors certified the seat's timeout at 81-84 s and, in the same breath, removed it from the group by the table's word (*silent in the table's group for 33 s*), the library deleting the entry at once (a kick at the founder, *exit type 6*; the word at the other member, *exit type 4*), and no timeout deletion followed -- the runs before the certified-seat reader existed, `run142530-3` and `run144026-3`, certified at 82 s and waited for the library's timeout at 105 s. `run143721-3` (the founder's kick without the word at 46 s): the target and the third seat each logged *a kick without the table's word is ignored* and kept the seat, the table played thirteen hands, and the founder's own view alone lost the seat. `run143025-3` (a joiner leaving before the first hand): given back at 16.1 s by its QUIT, nothing left to drop. `run143443-3` failed on the bed before the certificate (the invite dance; S1-DZ).

**Guard.** `tools/build-tox.ps1`'s marker for `patches/0034`, the runs in point 5, the S1-DY row.

**Amended 2026-09-16 (`S1-FZ`).** A key removed for good is refused by `peer_add`, and a sync response that still names it is skipped (`patches/0038`): the sync reader took the refusal for an impossible value and aborted the client, a founder dying four seconds after giving a silent seat back (`run153101-3`).

## D-046 — a wait is not for ever: the question about an unreachable opponent comes back

**Decided 2026-09-12, the owner's ruling** (*"když stisknu Wait, tak by se nemělo vyřazovat z tox skupiny;
ale nesmí vzniknout nový deadlock, tzn. vyskakovací okno o odpojeném peeru se musí po krátkém (několik
desítek sekund) čase objevit znova"*).

1. **Pressing *Wait* removes nobody from the table's group**, and never did: the client removes a member only
   on the table's word (D-045) -- a certificate at three seats or more, or the roster before the first hand --
   and heads-up there is no certificate (D-007). What takes a seat out of the group after an outage is the
   library's own timeout, 58 s without a packet, at every member alike; the seat comes back by an invitation
   (S1-EB) or by the library's own reconnection to the address it last knew.
2. **The question comes back.** S1-CX asked *wait for them, or end the game and leave the table* once per
   episode. Now a player who chose to wait is asked again `OPPONENT_ASK_AGAIN_MS` = 30 000 later if the
   opponent is still out of reach, and again after that, the log line with it; a reading that reaches the
   opponent ends the episode as before, and D-032's count of returns is unchanged (an episode is one absence,
   however many times it was asked about).
3. **Measured.** The unit test (`a_heads_up_opponent_that_cannot_be_reached_is_said_and_asked_about`): a dismissed question is not asked again at once and comes back after `OPPONENT_ASK_AGAIN_MS`, said again in the log; the window itself was not driven -- the re-ask is the app's tick and thirty seconds of wall clock. Point 1 on the bed: in all three S1-EB runs the seat left the group by the library's timeout alone (*exit type 1*) and nothing here removed it.

**Guard.** `a_heads_up_opponent_that_cannot_be_reached_is_said_and_asked_about` (`src/app/mod.rs`), the S1-EB row.

## D-047 — the fourth absence is the last: out of the table's group and of the table

**Decided 2026-09-12, the owner's ruling** (*"v pravidle 3x a dost: po třetím pokusu o reconnect po výpadku linky
se po čtvrtém pokusu má status sit out -- ale to nestačí, musí být kompletně vyhozen z tox skupiny a ze stolu ten
peer se špatným připojením k internetu, nebo to může být peer, který schválně narušuje hru"*).

1. **The rule.** D-032 counts a seat's returns; at `MAX_RETURNS` the table declined to readmit it and it sat out as the
   tournament's dead seat, posting and draining (§8.3). Now a seat **certified absent with `MAX_RETURNS` returns behind
   it** -- its fourth absence -- is out of the table for good: at that hand's boundary its chips leave the table
   (`stack_at_hand_start` is zero from hand `k+1`), so every rule treats it as busted -- not dealt in, no blinds, no return
   (a busted seat cannot return) -- and the tournament goes on among the seats with chips, down to heads-up, or ends. The
   `Opening` carries the seats out (`out`, beside `returns`); every seat derives the same from the same certificates and
   nothing new is said on the wire.
2. **Out of the group, for good.** At the certificate every member gives the table's word with *for good* (D-045,
   `patches/0034`): the seat's every entry is dropped, the key is refused for the group's life, and the seat leaves the
   driver's roster, so the founder never offers the group to it again -- a fresh key needs an invitation (S1-EB) -- and
   its friendship idles out with the others no table needs. Silence is no condition here: a seat certified four times
   over is out whether its line is bad or its play is. The felt draws it as a seat that left.
3. **The seat's own client is told, and its window says so** (the owner, the same evening: *"GUI vyhozeného klienta by
   mělo informovat vyskakovacím oknem, že byl kicknut ze hry pro špatné internetové připojení a že jeho hra na tomto
   stole byla trvale ukončena, kde bude k dispozici tlačítko pro uzavření okna se stolem"*). A client that holds the
   fourth certificate knows at once. One whose line was down is told by the table's word itself: every client's lobby
   answer (D-040) carries, for the tables it sits at, the certificate of each seat out for good (`OutWord`: table, key,
   seat, hand, certificate; at most `SNAPSHOT_MAX_OUT` = 4 an answer), and the seat's own client verifies it against
   the table's roster from the bytes alone (`certificate_names`) -- nobody's authority, the founder's included, is what
   it rests on. A rejoin from a record is refused with the reason (reject code 9, `OutForGood`). The window then says
   *you were removed from this table after your fourth absence: your connection dropped too often, and the table plays
   on without you; your game at this table is over for good*, with one button, *Close the table*, and holds the table
   until it is pressed; a headless client leaves at once.
4. **Heads-up** is D-032 point 2, unchanged: no certificate at two seats; the survivor is told the game ends and leaves.
5. **Measured.** run195328-3 (three seats, the third seat's internet gone four times, 60 s every 140 s): at the fourth certificate (492-495 s, hand #51) both survivors kept the word (*the word about seat 2 is kept for its client's asking: 1127 bytes of hand #51*); the removed seat, still cut from the table's group but asking the lobby, read the word in a survivor's answer at 510 s, verified it against the roster (*certified by seats {0, 1} at hand #51, carried in the lobby answer of ...*) and, headless, left the table; its two later requests to sit again from its record were refused with the reason (*the founder says no: this seat was removed after its fourth absence; the game at this table is over for good*). 56 hands finished at the survivors on one genesis; the window's popup is covered by the unit tests of the view, the bed having no window. Before it, run183643-3 (three seats, the third seat's internet gone four times, 60 s every 140 s from 40 s): the survivors certified the seat's timeout at 78 s, 217 s, 359 s and 499 s, and it came back by a return certificate at 114 s, 248 s and 389 s (three returns, 4-11 s after each line's return); the fourth certificate landed with three returns behind it and both survivors said *seat 2 is out of the table for good after its fourth absence (D-047)* at 496-499 s; the library refused its key from then on (*a key the table's word removed for good is not added again*), no invitation reached it after its line came back at 520 s, and every one of the seventeen hands from 500 s to the end opened with seats [0, 1]; 62 hands finished at the survivors on one genesis.

**Guard.** `table::hand::the_fourth_absence_takes_the_seat_out`, `three_returns_are_the_limit`; the harness's
`-OfflineEvery`.

## D-048 — the table window after PokerTH's, in its Green Casino style

**Built 2026-09-13 at the project owner's instruction** (*"Napodob GUI hracího stolu pokerového klienta PokerTH co
nejvěrněji, jak vizuálně, tak funkčně ... Použij styl stolu Green Casino -- nevymýšlej nové prvky GUI navíc"*, with his
description of the table, the seats, the centre, the action bar, the side panels and the sounds; *"Vzhled hracích karet
ponech úplně beze změny"*; *"Nechat tam hlášku uprostřed stolu o technických informacích před zahájením hry"*; and, the
same day, *"všechny chybové hlášky ze starého GUI tam musí fungovat v novém GUI"*). The source is PokerTH at commit
`944e8b83`: the QML client (`src/gui/qt6-qml`) for the layout and the pieces, `data/gfx/qml/table/greencasino/` for the
style and its `preview.png` for the look. `assets/pokerth/PROVENANCE.md` names every file taken, its source and its terms.

1. **Where things are is PokerTH's.** `gui::table::seats` ports `seatlayout.js`: up to ten seats on PokerTH's oval with
   the hero at the bottom, the opponent box 114 by 84 and the hero's 142 by 96 scaled by the same bisection, the board's
   five slots with the pot badge above it, the pucks beside their boxes, a portrait layout for tall windows. The table
   picture fills the window, cropped around the board.
2. **What things look like is Green Casino's.** `gui::table::style` draws the style XML's accent and the QML theme's
   colours, the boxes' gradient and shadow, the action badges, the clock bar, the turn glow, the winner's frame and
   badge, the pot and bet chips, the quick bet buttons, the slider and the four action buttons stop for stop from their
   SVGs, in PokerTH's font (Inter). The icons are PokerTH's SVG files, filled at their shown size by `gui::table::icons`.
   The cards are not restyled: `gui::table::paint` keeps only the card face and back, byte for byte as before.
3. **The owner's words win over the picture where they differ**, and the code says so where it departs: the dealer and
   blind pucks are gold chips, a bet or a raise wears a gold badge, a seat's bet stands above its box, the avatars are
   round with the player's initial.
4. **The bar is `GameActionBar`.** Fold, Check or Call with its amount, Bet or Raise with its amount; the amount field, a
   third of the pot, half, the pot, all-in and the slider; *Manual*, *Auto Check/Call* and *Auto Check/Fold*; an action
   chosen before the turn is kept and played when the turn comes, and a call whose amount changed under the pointer is
   held for a second.
5. **The top of the window is PokerTH's.** The top bar: the door leaves the table (the old window's *Exit*, which asks
   first), the trophy opens the table's ranking by chips, the gear opens the sound settings. The status bar: the chips in
   the pot and in front of the seats on the left, the table's name in the middle with the blinds under it (the old
   window's), the street, the game and the hand on the right.
6. **The side panels are `GameSidePanel`.** The chat on the left is the seats' chat of D-030 with an unread count on its
   button; the log on the right writes each hand in PokerTH's words (*## Game: 1 | Hand: 12 ##*, *Alice posts big blind
   ($20)*, *Bob calls $20.*, *--- Flop --- [...]*, *Carol shows [...] - "two pair"*, *Carol wins $140*), and its *Odds*
   tab is the hero's odds of D-030 point 2.
7. **The sounds are PokerTH's fourteen.** Every seat's action; the turn warning three seconds before this client's own
   decision runs out, on a clock of four seconds or more; the blind raise by its level (1-2, 3-4, 5 and up); a player
   sitting down before the game; the game ready; a lobby line that names this client. PokerTH at `944e8b83` plays
   `dealtwocards.wav` from nowhere; here it plays when the hero's cards arrive. The settings are PokerTH's: on or off,
   volume 1 to 10, and four categories, kept in the settings file as an optional field an older file reads without.
   Windows plays them through WinMM; elsewhere the client is silent.
8. **PokerTH's note about a player.** A right-click on a seat: a rating of up to five stars and a note, kept in the
   profile under the player's application key (never the name, `PROTOCOL.md` section 4.3), never sent anywhere; the
   stars show under the name.
9. **Two more things the node tells the window**, local events and nothing on the wire: what each seat did (the
   action, the chips it put in, its total, whether it went all in, whether the table's certificate did it for the seat)
   and the application key of each seat.
10. **Nothing the old window said is lost**: the words over the felt before the first hand, the heads-up question
    (S1-CX, D-046) with *Wait* and *Leave the table*, *Out of the game* with *Close the table* (D-047), *Line down*
    (S1-EH), the seats off the line (S1-EI), the showdown's shown hands (S1-DO), the chips' flights, the preview banner,
    *Mute* and *Unmute*.
11. **Not taken, because nothing here stands behind them:** PokerTH's emoji reactions, spectators, private messages,
    forum news, the web table statistics and the zoom.
12. **The odds and the chat beside the action bar** (the owner, the same day, on a screenshot of a live table: the
    odds *in the bottom right corner*, *shown or hidden in the settings, shown by default*, *it must follow the
    window's size so it stays in that area*, *shrink its height so it does not cover the seated players*, no *Odds*
    heading, and *in the same way the chat in the left corner*). `corner_rect` gives each corner from the bar to the
    window's edge and down to the bottom, at most 380 points wide and at least 150, reaching up to 36 points past the
    bar's top; every seat's box and puck in the way lowers its top, so the panel grows shorter instead of covering a
    seat, and it is left out only when not even its first line fits. The right corner holds the hero's hand and its
    likeliest improvements, as many rows as fit; the left one holds the table chat with its line to type in, and
    stands down while the big chat panel is open, so there is one place to type. Two switches in both settings
    dialogs, `show_odds` and `show_chat`, optional fields an older settings file reads as shown.
13. **The winner blinks** (the owner, the same day: *in PokerTH the winner's place blinked with the WINNER
    label*). PokerTH's widget client, `gametableimpl.cpp`'s `postRiverRunAnimation5`, hides and shows the winner
    ten times at `winnerBlinkSpeed`; here the winner's gold frame, its glow and its *WINNER* badge go off and on
    ten times at 210 ms and then stay (`winner_blink_on`).
14. **The status bar says the hand's blinds.** It showed the table's starting blinds for the whole tournament.
    `NodeEvent::HandBegan` now carries the blinds the hand's `HAND_INIT` derived from the schedule, and the blind
    raise sound follows them instead of reading the posted bets, where a short stack's all-in blind looked like
    a level.
15. **Out of chips, the place** (the owner: *when I run out of chips after a hand, a window saying what place I
    finished in, with leaving the table or watching while players are still playing*). At a settled hand where
    this seat's chips went to zero, the place is the number of seats still holding chips plus one, and of the
    seats busted in the same hand the ones that began it with more finish ahead. The window says the place,
    offers *Watch the table* while two or more still play, and *Leave the table*; the log says it too.
16. **The winner is congratulated, and both windows wait ten seconds** (the owner, on a screenshot of the
    second-place window: *this message, titled that I am the winner, with congratulations, for the winner of
    the tournament, ten seconds after, so the winning hand can be looked at*). The last seat holding chips at
    the end of a hand two or more seats played gets *You won the tournament!* and *Congratulations! You finished
    in 1st place.* with *Leave the table*. That window and the place window both open
    `FINISH_WINDOW_DELAY_MS` = 10 000 ms after the deciding hand ended, which covered the showdown before.

**Guard.** `gui::table::seats`, `gui::table::style`, `gui::table::bar`, `gui::table::icons`, `gui::table` (the view, the
phases, the blind seats, the badge's pop, `both_corners_stay_in_their_corners_at_every_size` over seven window sizes
and two to ten seats, `a_seat_in_a_corner_makes_the_panel_shorter_not_hidden`), `app::tablelog`, `sound`,
`storage::notes`, `storage::settings` (`a_file_from_before_the_odds_switch_shows_the_odds`),
`gui::render::both_themes_get_the_same_palette`; `p2p-poker --table-preview` draws the window from the sample hand with no
node (`--preview-seats N`, `--preview-panels`, `--preview-over`, `--preview-note`, `--preview-gone`, `--preview-out`,
`--preview-line`, `--preview-absent`, `--preview-sound`, `--preview-ranking`, `--preview-player-note`, `--preview-odds`,
`--preview-chat`), each photographed against `preview.png`, and the corners at 760 by 560, 1000 by 720, 900 by 1000 and
1800 by 980 with two, six and ten seats.

**Amended 2026-09-16 (`S1-FW`, the owner's word).** The hero's decision clock is under its name, left of its stack, and no longer in the strip above its box; a seat's clock is drawn at every turn of its own, and an opponent deciding has it where its last word was. `--preview-reraised` draws the hero raised, re-raised and deciding again.

**Amended 2026-09-16 again, the owner's word** (*"deaktivuj v GUI zobrazování SB a BB buttonů, stačí mi dealer button"*). The blinds' pucks are not drawn: beside the boxes stands the dealer's puck alone. `gui::table::blind_seats`, its test and `style::Puck` went with them; `style::dealer_puck` draws the one left.

## D-049 — a seat whose clock runs out sits out until the player is back

**Built 2026-09-13 at the project owner's instruction** (*"Hráč, který se nerozhodne v časovém limitu, získá status
sit out, tzn. že když bude na řadě, tak dá jeho klient instantně check / fold, dokud svým návratem sit out nezruší
stiskem tlačítka v GUI. To tlačítko se zobrazí místo těch tří akčních tlačítek ... Ostatní hráči u toho hráče uvidí
nápis sit out. Zařiď, ať tato indikace je spolehlivě aktualizovaná a aby tam nezůstala (například po ztrátě packetů)
jako duch, i když hráč zruší svůj status sit out nebo přejde do offline"*).

1. **The rule.** When this client's own clock runs out on its own turn and it checks or folds for its player
   (D-034), the seat **sits out**: from then on the node checks or folds **at once** on every turn of the seat,
   and nothing else of the hand changes -- the seat is dealt in, posts its blinds, shows its cards and signs its
   own actions, so no certificate is spent on it and no absence is counted (D-032, D-047). It ends only when the
   player presses *I'm back*, which replaces Fold, Call and Raise in the window (`NodeCommand::SitBack`); a turn
   armed at that moment gets its clock back. `--autoplay`, the measurement flag, never sits a seat out.
2. **What the others see is the seat's own word, carried by the table's group.** Tox groups keep a status per
   member: NONE, AWAY or BUSY. A seat sitting out sets its status in the table's group to AWAY, and back to NONE
   when it is back. The library sends a status as a lossless broadcast to the members, and every member
   exchanges it again with each peer it connects or reconnects to, so a status lost with a connection comes
   back with the connection. Belt and braces, the seat says its status again every 20 s
   (`AWAY_RESAY`), changed or not, and sets it on every fresh copy of the group it takes. No protocol message
   and no toxcore patch: the status is part of the group protocol the library already speaks.
3. **No ghost.** The driver reads each member's status in the same sweep that reads whether the member is in
   the group and how long it has been quiet, and takes it from the seat's most recently heard entry (S1-DU: a
   seat back under a fresh key leaves a dead entry behind for a while). The node says `away` with each seat's
   link reading, and only for a seat on the line (D-041, S1-DX); the window keeps the word only while the seat
   is on the line and draws nothing of it for a seat that is not. So a seat that goes offline shows as off
   the line, not as sitting out; one that comes back sitting out is said to sit out again once the group
   holds it; and one that is back is said to play within one sweep of the group hearing it.
4. **Display only.** The status is never evidence and never enters a hash (D-012): it is what a seat says
   about itself, read from the member the table's evidence says the seat is. A member cannot set another's.
5. **The harness** gained `-AfkAt`, `-BackAt` and `-AfkNode` (`P2P_POKER_AFK_AT`, `P2P_POKER_BACK_AT`): from
   `-AfkAt` a node stops autoplaying, so its own clock runs out as a player's does who left the keyboard; at
   `-BackAt` it presses *I'm back*. Every node's log says *seat N sits out by the table's group* and *seat N
   plays again by the table's group* when the reading changes.

6. **Measured**, three seats on this machine, every node autoplaying but the one told to stop. **run155209-3**
   (`-AfkAt 70 -BackAt 200`; the group took 110 s to form, so the seat's first turn came late): its own clock ran
   out once, at 156 s, and it sat out; its next thirteen actions went out *at once*, each about 0.2 s after the
   action before it, and none was autoplay; the other two seats said *seat 2 sits out by the table's group* 4.9 s
   and 9.1 s after, and *plays again* 2.8 s and 5.0 s after the seat was back at 200 s; one of each at each seat,
   24 hands on one genesis, no hand aborted. The 9.1 s was the driver's five-second sweep at both ends, so the
   status is now set when the command arrives. **run160018-3** (`-AfkAt 150 -BackAt 380`, and the sitting seat's
   internet cut at 230 s for 45 s): the word reached the others 1.4 s and 6.0 s after the seat sat out at 190 s;
   at the cut both said *seat 1 link: not on the line* about 22 s later and nothing about sitting out; when the
   seat was in the group again, at 295 s, both said *seat 1 sits out by the table's group* in the same second as
   *on the line* -- the group's word read again, the seat still sitting out; at 385 s *plays again* came 0.7 s and
   5.1 s later, and nothing more to the end. 55 hands; the cut seat came back behind and rejoined from the
   table's copies (D-038), sitting out as it had left.

7. **At once** (the owner, the same day: *the sit-out status must go immediately after I'm back; it has a big
   delay*). The delay was at the far end: a status arrived at once, but the driver published it on its
   five-second sweep and the node read it on its two-second tick. Now the driver takes a member's status the
   moment the library reports it (`tox_callback_group_peer_status`), the node looks at the group's word every
   250 ms, and the player's own window drops the word at the click, before the node answers; the sweep and the
   tick still read everything again, so a missed callback costs seconds and not a ghost. Measured **run175118-3**
   (`-AfkAt 90 -BackAt 200`): the other two seats said *sits out* 0.1 s and 0.2 s after the seat sat out, and
   *plays again* 0.1 s and 0.2 s after it was back, against 0.7 to 9.1 s before; 32 hands on one genesis.

**Guard.** `app::table::sitting_out_and_the_groups_word_reach_the_window` (the word shown, dropped off the line
without a *back*, taken back); the bar's *I'm back* photographed from `--table-preview --preview-sitout`; the
harness's `-AfkAt`/`-BackAt`.

**Amended 2026-09-15 (`S1-FS`).** The clock whose running out sits a seat out is one the player could see: a turn that stood when a restarted client took the hand up again runs the whole clock from the take-up, and a turn heard after its time has ten seconds from when it was heard (`D-034`). The fold of a seat back without its card material is `D-033`'s and sits nobody out.

## D-050 — a hand that may muck waits for its player, who may show it

**Built 2026-09-13 at the project owner's instruction** (*"přidej na showdown tlačítko pro možnost ukázat své karty
(v časovém limitu délky showdownu), v případě, když karty nemusím ukazovat (muck), ve stejném stylu jako je tlačítko
I'm back"*; the same day: *"7 s je moc dlouhá doba, stačí 3 sekundy, a také možnost do nastavení auto muck
defaultně zapnuté"*, *"a aby se muck zobrazovalo u hráčů v GUI podobně jako bet, raise, fold, call"*, and *"vygenerovat
a přidat krátkou zvukovou událost pro muck"*).

1. **What was there.** At a showdown the seats speak in order, and each client decides for its own hand when the
   seats ahead of it have spoken: it shows when it is first, when anybody is all in, or when nothing shown beats
   it, and otherwise it mucks at once (D-021, the owner's *if they find out they have lost, they muck*). Nobody was
   asked.
2. **The rule now.** A setting decides, *Auto muck*, on by default: on, a hand the rules let muck is mucked at
   once, as before. Off, it waits for its player instead: the window offers *Show cards* in place of Fold, Call
   and Raise, with the seconds left, in the style of *I'm back*. Pressed, the client sends `SHOWDOWN_REVEAL`; not
   pressed, it sends `SHOWDOWN_MUCK` when the time is up. Both are the messages the showdown always had; only when
   the muck is sent changed, and nothing about who may muck. The setting is in both settings windows and reaches
   the node as `NodeCommand::SetAutoMuck` at start and on every save.
3. **How long.** `SHOW_WINDOW_MS` = 3 000 ms (a first build waited the table's 7 s pause; the owner: too long), cut to
   what the showdown stage's budget (`crypto_step_timeout_ms`, 30 s) leaves after `SHOW_MARGIN_MS` = 8 000 ms, counted
   from when this client saw the stage open. The seats behind a waiting hand wait on it inside that one budget, so
   a later waiting hand can get less, and below `SHOW_WINDOW_MIN_MS` = 2 000 ms a hand mucks at once. A seat sitting out
   (D-049) has nobody to ask and mucks at once; a measurement run (`--autoplay`) never waits.
4. **Where it lives.** The engine holds the decision (`Hand::hold_muck_for_the_player`, `muck_held_until`,
   `show_held`, `muck_held_now`), the node keeps the timer (`TableRun::show_by`), says
   `NodeEvent::ShowdownChoice` and takes `NodeCommand::ShowCards`; the window reads the time left.
5. **The harness** gained `-HoldMuck show|muck` (`P2P_POKER_HOLD_MUCK`): an autoplay run whose hands wait as a
   window's do, then show at once or let the window run out.

6. **Everybody sees a muck.** At a showdown -- somebody showed -- every seat that held its cards to the end and
   showed none wears a *Muck* badge where its last action's badge was, in the greys of cards face down; the log says
   *Bob mucks.* between the shown hands and the winners; and a short sound plays. PokerTH has no muck and no sound
   for one, so `assets/sounds/muck.wav` is this project's own, generated from a fixed seed by
   `tools/make-muck-sound.py` so the same bytes can be made again. The first one hit at once with most of its
   energy a low tap under 300 Hz, and the owner found it aggressive; of four softer candidates made in the character
   of PokerTH's deal sound he chose **B, a soft flick**: the swell of a sliding card and a gentle, darker flick at
   75 ms, nothing below 300 Hz and nothing above 5 kHz to speak of, 0.22 s, peak -12 dBFS and about 7 dB quieter
   than the first. It plays under *Game actions*.
7. **Measured**, three seats autoplaying with `-HoldMuck`. **run170847-3** (the 7 s build, `muck`): every wait said
   6 999-7 000 ms and ended in the muck; the hand was over 0.3 s later, or after a second seat's own wait in the
   same showdown (hands #1 and #10, about 14 s together); 16 hands at every node on one genesis, none aborted.
   **run172111-3** (3 s, `muck`): nineteen waits of 2 999-3 000 ms, each ended in the muck and the hand over
   0.1-0.3 s after, or about 3 s after where a second seat waited in the same showdown; 20 hands at every node
   on one genesis. **run172536-3** (3 s, `show`): thirty-three waits, each shown within the same tenth of a
   second, not one muck; 28 hands at every node on one genesis, none aborted.

**Guard.** `table::hand::a_hand_that_may_muck_waits_for_its_player` (two peers to a showdown until both outcomes
come up: the waiting hand shown on both tables, or mucked on both), `app::table::the_showdown_choice_reaches_the_window`,
`app::tablelog::a_mucked_hand_is_said_shown_and_heard`, `sound::every_sound_is_sixteen_bit_stereo_pcm` (the muck
among them), `storage::settings` (Auto muck on for a file from before it); the bar and the badge photographed
from `--table-preview --preview-show`.

## D-051 — the table's group holds its seats alone, and a member that floods it is cut off by every member it floods

**Decided 2026-09-13, the owner's rulings** (*"chránit tox skupinu proti DDoS od rogue peera, který se snaží zahltit
kanál generovaným provozem (šumem) -- bezpodmínečný permanentní kick; a také v tox skupině stolu nesmí být cizí
nehrající peer; samozřejmě bezpečný kick, který nesmí být zneužíván k vyhození legitimního hráče u stolu jedním
peerem"*; *"vyřešit i situaci, kdy více než jeden peer se snaží o DDoS a je jasné a pravděpodobné, že nebudou
hlasovat pro kick"*; *"pokud to nebude řešitelné bezpečně, tak aspoň poctivým peerům zobrazit hlášku, že stůl není
bezpečný, s doporučením odejít"*).

1. **Every member says which seat it is, in the group's own member name.** A seat's client names itself in the
   table's group with its *binding* (`table::membership`): a four-byte tag, its application key, and its signature
   over `h("p2p-poker v1 member-binding", [chat_id, member_key])` -- one hundred bytes, the library's limit for a
   name being 128. It is set the moment the group exists, before the founder's first invitation and before a
   joiner's first handshake, so every member reads it with the member's own peer information, and again at the
   sweep if the first try found nothing to sign. Every member checks it against the key the group itself holds
   for that member, so a copy of another member's binding does not verify. A member bound to a seat is paired by
   its binding, and a pairing read off carried traffic -- which anybody can carry, `S1-EP` -- no longer moves it.
   Nothing new is said on the wire: the name is the library's own field.
2. **A member that is no seat is removed by every member, on its own check.** Cut off at once: a member whose name
   is a binding made for another member or another group; one bound to this client's own seat; one bound to an
   application key the ratified roster does not seat. After `NAME_GRACE` (ten seconds): a member with no binding at
   all. A member bound to a key the forming roster does not name yet waits for the roster, and is cut off the
   moment the roster is ratified without it -- a joiner's roster can lag the founder's invitation by as long as
   the mesh takes (`S1-DP`). *Cut off* is D-045's removal for good, taken on this client's own evidence: allowed
   to be kicked, kicked where this client is the founder, dropped, its member key refused for the group's life.
   No member's word is involved, so no member can have a seat removed this way: a seat's own binding verifies
   at every member. Our groups are private, so a stranger comes in only by a member's invitation -- which any
   member may send -- and a table where that keeps happening is not safe (point 5).
3. **A member that floods the group is cut off by every member it floods, on that member's own count, and its seat
   is barred there.** The driver counts each member's traffic before anything is spent on it (`Meter`): more than
   `FLOOD_SHORT_PACKETS` = 6 000 packets or `FLOOD_SHORT_BYTES` = 3 000 000 bytes within `FLOOD_SHORT_S` = 10
   seconds, or `FLOOD_LONG_PACKETS` = 15 000 packets or `FLOOD_LONG_BYTES` = 7 500 000 bytes within
   `FLOOD_LONG_S` = 60, is a flood; so is `NOISE_LIMIT` = 16 points within a minute of traffic no client of this
   build sends -- a fragment the reassembler refuses (1 point), a whole message that is not a signed event or does
   not verify under the key inside it (4), a group text message, private message or private packet (4). The
   flooder is cut off, and its bound seat is barred at this client for the table's life: every other entry the
   seat holds goes with it, and any member key bound to it later goes the moment its name is read. **No vote, no
   founder, no other member is involved**: the evidence is the traffic that reached this client from that key,
   so it cannot be made about another member, and several flooders are cut off each on its own count. And while
   a table's inbox is three quarters full, a member sending more than `INBOX_LOUD` = 100 packets in a second and
   twice anybody else waits its turn, so one member cannot crowd the others' events out before its count trips.
4. **The table puts a flooder out for good by its ordinary word, carrying the cause.** A seat cut off by the other
   seats is quiet at every one of them, so at its next stage their clocks run out and D-036's certificate names it
   -- and every flooder quiet at that stage together -- from the votes of the seats not named. **The flooders'
   votes are never needed, because they are the seats named.** Each vote about a seat its voter's client cut off
   carries `n(6) cause` = `CAUSE_FLOOD` = 1 (`PROTOCOL.md` §8.3). The cause is part of the subject -- a vote without
   it encodes and hashes exactly as it did before -- so a certificate completes only with the cause every voter
   signed; a seat named with it is out of the table for good at that boundary exactly as D-047's fourth absence:
   its chips leave the table, it is not dealt in and cannot return, the table's word removes it from the group for
   good, and its own client is told by the lobby answer, whose certificate says why (*removed from this table for
   flooding its connection*). One client's measurement alone completes nothing, and a voter that signs the cause
   to one peer and not to another completes only what the others signed. A client votes once about a seat at one
   stage, so a seat it cuts off after voting is voted about with the cause at its next stage; and it votes for no
   return of a seat it cut off.
5. **Where the table cannot put them out, its honest players are told it is not safe, and leaving is recommended**
   -- the owner's fallback. The window says *This table is not safe* with the reason, *Leave the table* and *Stay*,
   and asks again every two minutes while it holds; a headless client logs it. It holds when: heads-up, the other
   seat flooded (nothing at two seats puts a player out); the seats this client cut off are half the seats in the
   hand or more (no certificate forms, D-036 point 2); a seat cut off here is still in the game two minutes later
   (it floods only some players, or a player will not vote); three strangers were removed within ten minutes
   (somebody keeps letting them in).
6. **A bad link is not a flood, and cannot be mistaken for one -- the owner's question.** A poor connection loses
   packets and reorders them; it does not manufacture the traffic either meter counts. **The volume meter** is set
   far above what an honest seat sends at its heaviest: the re-send loop repeats at most sixty-four messages every
   five seconds and a seat back from an outage re-says its whole hand, and measured at ten seats with an outage the
   busiest member ever sent a small fraction of the limits (point 8) -- a retransmission burst lives inside that
   fraction, not near `FLOOD_SHORT_PACKETS`. **The noise meter** counts only malformed framing and bytes that are
   not a valid signed event, which a client of this build never produces: its re-sends are valid signed events
   (scored as nothing), a duplicate fragment is accepted silently rather than refused, and a bad link cannot forge a
   malformed packet either, because every group packet is decrypted under the sender's session key before it reaches
   the application (`decrypt_data_symmetric`) -- a packet a bad link corrupts is dropped at the transport and never
   reaches the meter. The one framing collision a reconnection could cause -- a leaving member's group id reused by
   the next member -- is closed by forgetting the leaver's half-built messages (`Reassembler::forget`). Measured: an
   honest seat is never cut off, through a full outage and its recovery burst (H0) and through a link that keeps
   dropping and re-sending (R1). A raw peer that is no client of this build can still be metered into a cut, which
   is a correct removal of a non-seat, not a false one.
7. **What this does not do.** It does not stop a flood at the socket: a member cut off here can still send packets
   the library refuses by key before decrypting them, which cost only that decryption. It does not make a seat that
   floods only some players provable to the others -- those players stop hearing it and are told the table is not
   safe (point 5). A false count at one honest client would cost the table its certificate about that seat, since
   that client's vote would carry a cause the others' do not -- which is why the limits sit where point 6 puts them.
8. **Measured**, single machine, the release binary with the fault harness, each prediction booked before the run.
   **`run214504-10`** (H0, ten honest seats, one seat's line cut 150-210 s): nobody cut anybody off, and the
   busiest member of the group ever sent **404 packets / 161 388 bytes in ten seconds and 756 / 290 549 in sixty**
   -- against limits of 6 000 / 3 000 000 and 15 000 / 7 500 000, so about a fifteenth of the packet limit at its
   heaviest, the outage's recovery burst included. **`run215255-4`** (F1, one flooder of four, 500 lossy junk
   packets a second from 120 s): the three honest seats each cut it off **0.4-0.8 s** after its first flood, on
   sixteen refused fragments; the certificate named it with `CAUSE_FLOOD` among `[0, 1, 2]` at its next stage
   (~156-160 s), it was out of the table for good, its own client read the word from a survivor's lobby answer at
   180 s and left, and the three played 32 hands on one genesis. **`run215904-5`** (F2, two flooders of five,
   junk frames): both cut off within a second of each other, **one joint certificate** named `[3, 4]` with the
   cause among `[0, 1, 2]`, both out for good, 30 hands on one genesis. **`run220445-4`** (F3, two of four flood,
   800 a second): cut off on the packet count (6 000 in 10 s) within 7-12 s; the two survivors said **the table is
   not safe** -- *2 of the 4 players flooded ... too few other players are left to put them out* -- within five
   seconds, no certificate forming because the voters did not outnumber the named; a barred seat's key, re-added by
   the library's own reconnection, was cut off on sight. **`run221411-3`** (S1, a stranger with no binding invited
   in at 108 s): removed by all three within **0.6 s** as no seat of the table, no honest seat touched, hands on
   one genesis. **`run223234-3`** (S2, a stranger named with a copy of a seat's binding): removed within **0.1-0.3 s**
   as *a binding made for another member* -- the copy does not verify against the stranger's own member key -- and
   never paired to a seat. **`run223646-2`** (F4, heads-up, the opponent floods): cut off in **3.3 s**, and the
   survivor told **the table is not safe -- at two seats nothing can put a player out**. **`run224044-6`** (R1, the
   owner's question: six honest seats, one link cut 100-125 s so its traffic stalls and catches up in a burst on
   return): **nobody cut off, no noise, no unsafe word**, the busiest member 134 / 47 012 in ten seconds, 24 hands
   on one genesis -- a bad link is not a flood.

**Guard.** `table::membership` (`a_binding_names_its_own_member_in_its_own_group_and_nothing_else`,
`a_flood_is_over_a_limit_and_honest_traffic_is_not`, `a_member_is_counted_over_both_windows_and_forgotten_after_the_long_one`),
`table::handwire::tests::a_vote_without_a_cause_is_the_vote_it_always_was`,
`table::hand::tests::seats_every_voter_cut_off_for_flooding_are_out_of_the_table_for_good`,
`a_flood_cause_one_voter_alone_names_completes_no_certificate`; the harness's `-FloodAt`/`-FloodNodes`/`-FloodKind`
and `-StrangerAt`/`-StrangerFlood`/`-StrangerName`.

## D-052 — the winner's word blinks at its seat, and says which pot it won

**Decided 2026-09-14, the owner's ruling** (*"chci, aby GUI stolu zvýraznilo hráče, který v showdownu získal pot,
nebo toho hráče, co vyhrál handu (všichni složili), aby u jeho místa blikalo winner (jak to dělá PokerTH), aby bylo
jasné, kdo vyhrál -- handu/pot: main pot nebo side pot nebo split remíza"*).

1. **One word, in the badge above the seat's box.** A seat that took chips at the settlement blinks its word in the
   gold pill over its own box for `WINNER_BLINK_STEP` x 10 (about two seconds) and then stays, which is PokerTH's
   `postRiverRunAnimation5` and the same clock the winner's gold frame already blinked on (D-048). That pill is the
   one D-048 drew *WINNER* in, and it now carries the word instead -- **one** label, in one place for every seat.
   A second badge in the seat's action slot was built first and thrown away on the photograph: at an opponent it
   said the same thing twice, and at this player's own seat, whose badges go in the strip above the box, it landed
   under the bet chip and could not be read at all. The action the seat last took is stale the moment the hand is
   settled, so it is no longer drawn over its cards either. Both roads to a win say it -- the showdown, and the hand
   everybody else folded out of.
2. **And it says which pot.** *Winner* alone is the whole truth only where the hand settled into one pot, and at a
   table with side pots it says nothing about which chips moved. So the word is read from the settlement's own
   pots: **Winner** (one pot, taken alone), **Split pot** (one pot, shared), **Main pot**, **Side pot**,
   **Main + side** (both), **Split main** and **Split side**. The order is the settlement's -- `HAND_COMPLETE`'s
   `n(0) pots` has the main pot first and each side pot after it -- and a pot whose `winners` holds more than one
   seat was split, which is the same evidence every seat has.
3. **The pots reach the window because the engine keeps them.** The settlement body goes with the step that carries
   it (`Step::Ended`), so `Hand::settled_pots` holds what it named -- each pot's size and its winners -- written
   where the settlement is applied and on the late road (`S1-CL`) alike. `NodeEvent::HandEnded` carries them as
   `PotEnd`, and the window's word is derived in `app::table::win_at`, where it is tested. **Nothing new is said on
   the wire**: these are the bytes the settlement already carried, taken one layer further up.
4. **A hand that named no pots still says *Winner*.** An abort moves no chip and names nothing; a window that heard
   only the end of a hand has no pots either. Where the settlement named none, the badge falls back to the chips
   that moved to the seat, which is what it showed before there were pots to name.
5. **A winner is a seat the settlement named, never a seat an amount moved to** (`S1-ER`, found in a real game the
   day this was built). The window used to mark the winner by the chips it saw move, and it worked out what moved
   by subtracting the last state the node had reported from the settled one -- which the node reported *after* the
   settlement, so the difference was zero and nothing was marked at all. What each seat gained is now the engine's
   own figure, read off where the settlement replaces the stacks (`Hand::settled_gain`), and the word is drawn from
   the pots, which name the winners outright.

**Guard.** `app::table::tests::the_winner_of_each_pot_is_named_at_its_seat` (one pot alone and shared, a main and a
side pot to different seats, and a seat that took both), `gui::table::tests::the_winner_blinks_five_times_then_stays`
(the blink itself, D-048), `app::table::tests::the_winner_survives_a_state_reported_after_the_settlement` (`S1-ER`:
the node's own order of events, which the preview cannot show); photographed from `--table-preview
--preview-winner`.

## D-053 — the client's log keeps what matters, and never grows past a megabyte

**Decided 2026-09-14, the owner's ruling** (*"logování do client.log je velmi spamující a nafukuje se rychle; to
bych chtěl inteligentně omezit na logování např. certifikací, bezp. incidentů od rogue peerů atd., a omezit velikost
souboru s logem na 1 MB"*).

1. **A drop list, not a keep list.** What leaves the file is the lobby's own bookkeeping -- peers appearing on the
   mesh, answers to lobby questions, dials, relays, addresses refused, a connection going direct, and (`S1-IO`) a
   connection **staying** relayed and the count of relays advertised in the DHT -- which is nearly
   all of the volume and none of the meaning: no table traffic rides any of it, and the status line already says
   what the lobby amounts to. Everything else is kept, so a line nobody thought of is still in the file when the
   next fault has to be diagnosed from it. That is the opposite of a keep list, and deliberately: a keep list
   loses exactly the line nobody predicted.
1b. **`S1-IM`: and the same judgement belongs to the pane the player reads.** The drop list guarded the file alone, while `AppState::note` wrote every line into `log` -- 500 of them -- which is what *Network details* shows (`D-067`). Measured over the seven runs kept for `S1-AA`: `found <peer> in the public lobby` was **44 % of all 505 957 lines**, naming 2 186 peers a hundred times each, so the pane could not hold one minute. A lobby peer is named once a session now; the count line beside it says the recurrence.
2. **And a keep list above it**, so a line that matters is never dropped for holding a word the drop list names:
   anything a decision tagged (`(D-0…`), every certificate, the table's word, and every word about a member
   flooding, cut off, removed, kicked, put out of the table or found to be no seat -- the security incidents the
   owner named.
3. **A line repeated is counted, not repeated.** Consecutive copies of one line are folded and the count written
   out when the next different line comes, so a loop costs one line and a number instead of a megabyte, and
   nothing is lost.
4. **One megabyte, and the newest half survives.** Past `LOG_FILE_MAX` = 1 048 576 bytes the file is cut to its
   last `LOG_FILE_KEEP` bytes at a line boundary. It used to be emptied at eight megabytes, which threw away
   precisely the lines a reader had just come to look at.
5. **The fold, the trim and the append are one step**, under the lock the fold needs anyway. This file is evidence,
   and both threads that write to it are the client's own: without that, two of them could find the file over its
   bound at once and cut it twice, and a line appended between a trim's read and its write would go with the trim.
   A poisoned lock is taken anyway -- a panic somewhere else must not stop the client logging.

**Guard.** `app::tests::the_client_log_keeps_what_matters_and_drops_the_lobby` (the real lines of a run, kept and
dropped, and a security line that holds a dropped word), `app::tests::the_log_file_is_trimmed_to_its_newest_half`.

## D-054 — the chat a rogue client writes: what a receiver allows, and what it costs its sender

**Decided 2026-09-14, the owner's ruling** (*"navrhni mi bezpečný systém, který nelze obejít úpravou klienta rogue
peerem, na ochranu chatu u herního stolu proti spamu, maximální počet znaků na zprávu, a taky se obávám, že to může
být vstupní vektor pro DDoS na zahlcení linky"* -- and, once the table's was done, *"mrkni i na lobby chat, jak ho
chránit taky"*).

**The principle.** A chat line is the one thing at a table that is written by somebody else's client, and that
client is the attacker's to rewrite. So **no rule may rest on the sender**: the caps in `say` are this build's own
courtesy and bind nobody, and every bound that matters is checked by the **receiver** against the bytes that
arrived. The other half is D-051's: a permanent punishment must never rest on one peer's word either, or the
protection is itself a weapon against a legitimate player. So the ladder ends where D-051's ends -- in the table's
joint certificate.

1. **Two budgets, and the order of them is the whole rule.** The **carrier's** budget is charged first, against the
   group member key the carrier itself reports for the bytes: a fact about who sent them, which no sender can claim
   to be. Nothing of the message is read until it is paid. The **seat's** budget is charged only *after* the
   signature verifies. It used to be charged before -- against the key in the envelope, which is a *claim* -- and
   that was a way to silence any player at the table: the key is public and sits in every roster, so one unsigned
   line under Alice's key every two seconds spent Alice's whole allowance and her own lines were dropped as *too
   much*, with nothing in any window to say why. `lobby.rs` had been bitten by exactly this against table adverts
   and says so at `admit_table`; the table's chat never got the lesson. (`S1-ES`.)
2. **What the budgets are.** Three lines held back and spent at once, then one line per two seconds
   (`LINE_BURST`, `LINE_EVERY_MS`) -- a burst because *nice hand* and *wp* half a second later is the shape of
   people talking, and a hard gate dropped the second half of every real exchange. And **2 048 B a minute**
   (`CHAT_BYTES_MAX`): the line budget bounds the *count* and says nothing about the weight, so a speaker inside it
   could still put thirty full-length lines a minute on a link that is carrying a hand. A person types a fraction
   of either.
3. **A line is one line of printable text** (`net::plaintext`), and so is a display name. No control character --
   256 bytes of newlines is eighty-five empty rows in the pane, bought with *one* message of an honest budget. None
   of the invisible characters that change the direction or the shape of what is around them: a right-to-left
   override turns the rest of the pane around. At most four combining marks on one base, at most 120 bases. This
   build cleans what its own player types to exactly this rule *before it signs*, so nothing honest is ever
   refused, and what is refused is a client that wrote its own. **`PROTOCOL.md` §7.7 required the control
   characters and the bidi overrides from the beginning and no code ever checked them** (`S1-ET`).
4. **A refusal is noise, and noise is D-051's business.** A spent budget is one point against the member that
   carried the bytes and anything else is four (`noise_points`), so a peer that spams the chat is cut off from the
   group by the same meter, and put out for good by the same joint certificate, as one that floods it with junk --
   it merely takes longer, which is the difference between eager and hostile. No new mechanism, no new
   punishment, and no single peer's word in either.
5. **The table's chat rides the table's group and nothing else.** It used to ride the table's GossipSub topic too.
   That topic's name is derived from the `table_id` in every advertisement, so **any peer of the network could
   publish into a table it has no seat at** -- bytes on every seat's link that D-051's meter never sees, because
   that meter counts what the *group* carries. It was also the one path on which no signature had been verified
   before a budget was charged. The group is the closed set of the table's members, every one bound to a seat
   (D-051), and it is metered. A `TABLE_CHAT` arriving on the topic is now refused and not forwarded. The cost is
   that a line cannot be said before the group is up, and the window says so.
6. **The window draws the seat, not the name.** A line used to be composed as *"{nickname} (seat {n})"* in one
   string, so a seat could call itself *Alice (seat 0)* and read as another player's line. The seat comes from the
   signature and is drawn first in the window's own hand; the name follows it, muted, as the decoration it is.
7. **The lobby, on the owner's second word.** Its per-peer budget is charged against the *forwarding neighbour*,
   and on a gossip mesh one speaker arrives through every neighbour it has -- twenty neighbours were twenty
   budgets, all of them somebody else's, and **nothing bounded what one speaker could put in the pane**. A budget
   per **author key** now is, charged after the signature: 12 lines a minute for chat, and 4 for presence, which
   finally reads `MAX_PRESENCE_PER_PEER_PER_MIN` -- a constant that had sat declared and unused with a comment
   saying it would be wrong to charge it to a neighbour and right to charge it to an author (`S1-EU`). Those maps
   are keyed by a key out of a message and a public lobby has no roster, so they are swept of spent windows past
   `BUDGETS_MAX`: a limiter that grows without bound is itself a way to exhaust the machine it defends.

8. **And this client holds itself to the budget it holds everybody else to.** Every receiver counts an
   over-budget line against the member that carried it, and enough of those is a flood by D-051's meter -- so a
   client that let its own player type faster than the rule would have that player cut off the table **for being
   chatty**, which is exactly the thing this must never do. The window refuses the line instead and says why, in
   the lobby as at the table. What is left over the budget is then a client that is not this one, which is the
   only thing the meter ever sees.

**Measured**, `C1` run104410-4, four seats, one of them spamming at 8 lines a second from 60 s with lines that are
well formed and correctly signed (`-ChatSpamAt 60 -ChatSpamNodes '3' -ChatSpamRate 8`; the harness broadcasts
directly, so it is a client that does **not** hold itself to §8's budget):

| | |
|---|---|
| the spam begins | 60.1 s |
| first refusal at each honest seat | 61.0 s, 61.6 s, 64.8 s -- `TooMuchCarried`, the carrier's budget, before a byte of the message was read |
| cut off from the group | 63.2 s, 63.8 s, 67.0 s -- three to seven seconds of spam, each seat on its own arithmetic |
| out of the table for good | 98.4 s, 98.9 s, 102.2 s, by the joint certificate with the flood cause, seats {0, 1, 2} at hand #6 |
| the spammer learns | 120.1 s, from the table's word in a lobby answer (D-047b) |
| honest seats cut, or lines refused | **none** |
| the note in the window | **one** per seat, not one per line |
| the hands | #1-#6 at one genesis on all four nodes; the spammer's chain diverges at #7, which is after it was removed |

**Guard.** `net::plaintext::tests` (seven: what people type is accepted, newlines and overrides and stacks are
not, and what the cleaner produces is what the checker accepts), `net::tabletalk::tests` (twelve, among them
`a_forged_line_cannot_silence_the_seat_it_names`, `the_carrier_pays_before_a_byte_is_read`,
`a_seat_may_say_three_at_once_and_then_one_every_two_seconds`, `a_minute_of_chat_is_bounded_in_bytes`,
`a_line_that_is_not_one_line_of_text_is_refused`), `net::lobbytalk::tests::one_author_is_bounded_however_many_neighbours_relay_it`
and `::a_lobby_line_and_a_name_are_one_line_of_text`.

## D-055 — what a lobby costs at scale: the arithmetic, the bounds it forces, and the score that isolates a flooder

**Decided 2026-09-14, the owner's rulings** (*"bacha na legitimní peery, když tam bude tisíce peerů a například stovky
otevřených stolů, aby se to neblokovalo. Rogue peery je potřeba izolovat proti šumu, DDoS atd."*; *"počet legálních
stolů by měl být prakticky neomezený, může jich tam být >>> tisíce"*; *"myslím, že těch tisíce stolů si odrežíruje
samotná libp2p síť a její interní limity a ochrany"*; *"klient by mohl mít vlastní limit, např. že zobrazí max 1000
otevřených stolů, aby nepřetekl"*, and *"ten limit zobrazených stolů sniž na úroveň, co vyvodíš jako optimální"*;
*"tisíce stolů tady neotestuji, bude muset stačit tvá statická analýza"*).

### 1. What libp2p carries for us, and what it cannot

libp2p routes: it maintains the mesh, suppresses duplicates by message id, gossips `IHAVE`/`IWANT` so a message
crosses the network without anybody flooding everybody, bounds a single message (`GOSSIP_MAX_TRANSMIT`), bounds
connections (`MAX_CONNECTIONS`, and memory at a quarter of the machine), and backpressures a peer that writes faster
than this client reads.

What it does **not** do -- and cannot, because it is the definition of the thing -- is decide that a subscriber of a
topic does not want a message published to that topic. **Every subscriber receives every message.** So the traffic a
client carries for the lobby is set by the number of tables in the world, not by how many it is looking at.

### 2. The arithmetic

A table re-advertises every `AD_REBROADCAST_MS` (thirty seconds), so `T` tables in the world are `T / 30` messages a second on
the lobby topic, and **each of them reaches every client**. A client that accepts one forwards it to its mesh, which
is `mesh_n - 1` = 7 peers. An advert is about 400 B on the wire.

| tables in the world | adverts a second, inbound | inbound | outbound (x7) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 80 | 2.7 | 1 KB/s | 7 KB/s |
| 340 | 11 | 4.5 KB/s | **32 KB/s** |
| 1 000 | 33 | 13 KB/s | 93 KB/s |
| 5 000 | 167 | 67 KB/s | 470 KB/s |
| 20 000 | 667 | 267 KB/s | 1.9 MB/s |

The same formula holds for presence on the chat topic, with `P` players in place of `T` tables.

### 3. Where it breaks, in the order it breaks

1. **`MAX_ADS_PER_PEER_PER_MIN`, at eighty tables.** The budget is charged per *forwarding neighbour*, and a neighbour
   relays for the whole mesh: at `T` tables it carries about `T / 4` adverts a minute. The value was **twenty**, which
   is reached at eighty tables. Past that an honest neighbour's adverts were dropped and the lobby quietly stopped being a
   list of the tables that exist -- no error, no log, just a shorter list. **This was the thing that would have
   blocked legitimate peers**, and it was an application rule, not anything of libp2p's.
2. **The line, at about a thousand tables.** 93 KB/s of upload, continuously, to relay a lobby the player is not
   looking at -- while playing a hand that costs a few hundred bytes a second. At five thousand tables it is
   470 KB/s. No limit fixes this: it is the cost of subscribing to one global topic, and it is paid by every client.
3. **`MAX_TRACKED_TABLES`, at four thousand.** Memory, and it was never the binding constraint: no wire of this design
   delivers four thousand live tables to one client.

### 4. What is set, and why

- **`MAX_ADS_PER_PEER_PER_MIN`, twenty to ninety.** It stops being a fairness rule (fairness is
  `MAX_ADS_PER_TABLE_KEY_PER_MIN`, four a minute per table, which scales with the network) and becomes a **cost
  ceiling**: 90 a minute against 8 neighbours is 12 adverts a second, which is the 32 KB/s relay budget of the table
  above and a lobby that stays complete to about **340 tables**. A neighbour past the ceiling is dropped and **not
  condemned** (`Ignore`, never `Reject`), because carrying a busy topic is not misbehaviour.
- **`MAX_TRACKED_TABLES`, four thousand down to 512.** The owner's own rule -- *the client shows at most N tables so it does not
  overflow* -- with the number derived rather than picked: 512 sits just above the ~340 the wire can honestly deliver,
  so the **wire** is the constraint and the store never silently drops something that did arrive. 512 rows are about
  half a megabyte. A lobby a person reads is filtered and paged; PokerTH shows dozens.
- **The window turns over** (the owner: *the displayed tables must be continuously replaced by others*). A full
  window used to displace whichever advert expired soonest, which is a rotation only by accident: a table that
  re-advertises briskly holds its slot for ever, so at a network bigger than the window the first few hundred tables
  heard were the only ones a player ever saw. The row that has been **shown longest** goes instead, so the window is
  a moving sample of the network.
- **Except the table this client is at**, which is held (the owner's exception): never displaced, and never taken by
  an expiry sweep. This matters more than it sounds -- a table that fills **stops advertising**, so the row under the
  player was the first one the sweep would have taken.
- **And the redraw has a pace** (the owner: *a simple optimisation compromise*). A full window gives up at most
  `ROWS_ROTATED_PER_MIN` = 50 rows a minute. Without it a network past the window redraws the whole list every
  **forty-three seconds** -- at a hundred thousand tables this client accepts about 716 adverts a minute it does not
  hold, against 512 rows -- and that number hardly moves with the size of the network, because it is set by what this
  client accepts rather than by what exists. Fifty a minute turns the window over in about ten minutes instead: the
  same arbitrary, evenly drawn, still-moving sample, only legible enough to click on. It governs **displacement, not
  arrival** -- a window with room takes every table at once, so an empty lobby fills in seconds -- and a table already
  held costs nothing to re-advertise. It does **not** reduce what arrives: those adverts still land on the link and
  are still thrown away, which only `S1-EX` reaches.
- **And a row is held only while it is actively true that this client plays there** (the owner's second rule, which
  changed the design). The first build held a row on a *join* and released it on a *leave*, which is a pair of events
  -- and an event can be missed: a join that is refused never becomes a table and never leaves one, so its hold would
  have outlived it and left a row nothing in the lobby could ever shift again, a ghost for as long as the client ran.
  The held set is therefore **derived**: every `HOLD_EVERY` (five seconds) the node replaces it wholesale with the
  tables it is at and holds a seat in. There is no *add one* and no *remove one* to get wrong, a hold cannot outlive
  its table by more than those five seconds, and the cost is a handful of keys out of at most four tables at a fifth
  of a hertz -- the 250 ms loop skips it on a single comparison, because the set is read only when the window is full
  or being swept and a hold a few seconds stale costs one row of 512 for a moment.

### 5. The score, which is what isolates a flooder

`NETWORK_STACK.md` §6.7 decided peer scoring was on from day one; **nothing ever switched it on** (`S1-EW`), so a
`Reject` cost its sender exactly nothing and a peer could be refused for ever without consequence. It is on now, with
one deliberate difference from the library's defaults: **every rate term is zero**. GossipSub's P₁–P₃b judge a peer
by how much it delivers, and this network's topics are quiet -- a table speaks once every thirty seconds. The
default P₃ expects twenty deliveries a window and squares the shortfall, which would graylist **every honest peer**
of a quiet lobby. That is the risk §6.7 refused to take (OQ-5), and zeroing those terms is what makes the rest safe.

What is left is P₄, the count of messages **this client itself refused**, at `-1 × count²` with the count halving
every second. A peer sending `r` refusable messages a second settles at `-(2r)²`:

| refusals a second | score | |
|---|---|---|
| one in ten seconds | -0.04 | two honest clients disagreeing costs nothing |
| one | -4 | still heard |
| 4.5 | -81 | **graylisted**: its RPCs are dropped unread |
| 50 | -10 000 | gone at once |

This works only because the verdicts are disciplined: everything that is about *this client's own budget or memory*
(`RateLimited`, `NotTaken`, `TooMuch`) is `Ignore` and never reaches the score, and only a finding about the message
itself is `Reject`. That distinction was already kept at every verdict in `run.rs`; it is now load-bearing.

Loopback is whitelisted against the IP-colocation penalty: every measured run this project has is ten clients on one
machine, and the default would have scored a bed run into the graylist as soon as it grew past ten.

### 6. What is still open: one global topic does not scale, and the fix is sharding

The owner wants tables to be **practically unlimited**, and §2 says plainly that one topic cannot do it: at 20 000
tables every client relays about 1.9 MB/s. The bounds above make the failure *safe and visible* -- the lobby degrades
to a rotating sample of about 340 tables instead of collapsing -- but they do not make it unbounded.

The fix is to stop subscribing every client to every table: **shard the advert topic** by the table's own key, a
founder publishing into its table's shard and a client subscribing only to the shards it can afford. Targeted search
("a 50/100 table") is unaffected -- it is D-040's question to peers, not the broadcast. This is `S1-EX`, and it is a
protocol change (§7.1's topic names), so it is booked rather than smuggled in. What follows is the design, written
down so that it is not re-derived from scratch when the day comes.

**A shard cannot be chosen for what is in it.** The shard comes from the table key, which is a public key: it has no
correlation with stakes, seats or preset, so *"subscribe to the shard with the 50/100 tables"* does not exist. A
client chooses only **how many** shards and **which arbitrary ones**, and everything else is D-040's question.

**The depth is measured, not guessed.** A client does not need to be told how many tables exist -- it can read it off
what it hears, because every table advertises once every thirty seconds:

> `T` is about (adverts a second) x 30 x (shards at my depth)

So: start at depth zero, which is the whole topic and today's behaviour, and a small network never leaves it. Measure
the inbound rate over half a minute. Over the budget -- the per-neighbour cost ceiling already derived above, twelve
adverts a second -- go one depth deeper and measure again; far under it with a window that will not fill, go
shallower. Hysteresis on both sides and at most one change a minute, so it cannot oscillate. The depth wanted for `K`
shards and a window of `MAX_TRACKED_TABLES` rows is the one nearest `T x K / rows`:

| tables | depth | tables a shard | four shards | inbound |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 000 | 4 bits (16) | 312 | a full window | 1.4 a second |
| 100 000 | 11 bits (2 048) | 49 | 195 rows | 6.5 a second |
| 2 000 000 | 16 bits (65 536) | 30 | 122 rows | 4 a second |

The ladder therefore has to go deeper than twelve bits -- at millions of tables a single twelve-bit shard is over the
budget on its own -- so the depths are every four bits: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16.

**How many shards is decided by connections, not by bandwidth.** A topic's mesh is built only from peers this client
is *connected to* that also subscribe to it, so each shard wants ten or twelve connections of the eighty this client
keeps. That is **four to six shards**, and the rest of the connection budget stays for the table's own traffic, the
relays and the DHT. It is also why sharding cannot be done by splitting the topic alone: with random peering the
expected mesh candidates for a shard are `80 x K / N`, which falls below `mesh_n_low` past about `13 x K` shards --
fifty-odd, whatever the size of the network. **Sharding requires a per-shard discovery key in the DHT** (the pattern
of `p2p-poker/main-lobby/v1`) so that a client dials peers *of its own shards* and its connections are chosen rather
than random.

**Which shards: arbitrary, and slowly rotating.** Not derived from this client's own key, which would pin a player to
one slice of the network for ever and hide the rest. Random, `K` at a time, one swapped for a fresh one every few
minutes -- which spreads the load evenly across clients, keeps the sample moving (the same rule as the redraw pace,
one storey up), and is subscribed **before** the old one is left so the list never goes blank.

**What "what N" costs, and how to avoid agreeing on it.** Too few shards is the firehose again; too many leaves a
shard with so few subscribers worldwide that its mesh cannot hold together. The way out is for a founder to publish
its advert at **every depth** (0, 4, 8, 12, 16 -- five publishes every thirty seconds, which is nothing) and for each
client to subscribe at the depth its own network needs. Nobody agrees on anything, a client of an older build keeps
working at depth zero, and publishing into a topic nobody subscribes to costs the founder nothing at all: with no
mesh there, it sends nothing.

**The two constants derived above are the inputs of that loop**, which is what makes it self-tuning: the cost ceiling
is the budget the depth regulates against, and the window's rows are the target the shard count regulates against.
Nothing further is configured.

### Built, 2026-09-14

`src/net/shard.rs` is the arithmetic -- the slice of a key at a depth, the ladder of depths, the estimate of the
network's size from what arrives, the depth with its hysteresis, and the choice of slices -- and `run.rs` is the wiring:
a founder publishes at every depth, a receiver takes an advert from whichever slices it listens to, the depth is
weighed on the housekeeping tick from half a minute of traffic, one slice is swapped for another every three minutes so
that four slices of a large network still walk across it, a new topic is subscribed to **before** the old one is left,
and each slice this client listens to is announced and looked for under its own DHT provider key. The default is depth
zero -- the whole lobby, exactly as before -- and a network small enough never leaves it.

**Measured**, `-LobbyDepth 8` holding every node at eight bits (256 slices, four each):

| | |
|---|---|
| `X1` run133239-4 | four seats already playing when the slices appeared: **442 hands**, one genesis at every seat. Slicing does not disturb a table that is running -- a table's own traffic never rode the lobby topic. |
| `X2` run133741-4 | four seats **from the start**, joining over 45 s. The table was found, formed and played: **424-426 hands**, hands #1-#4 at one genesis at all four. First hand at 36.7 s against X1's 22.2 s. |
| how it was found | by **D-040's question**, at every joiner, and by gossip at none: with four slices of 256 the chance a joiner holds the founder's slice is 1.6 %, and none did. |
| `X3` run134418-3 | the slices are arbitrary and each client's own: *depth 8 bit(s), listening to slice(s) 43, 51, 4a, 0b* / *20, 7b, 0c, df* / *40, 07, 0c, f7*. |

**What the bed can and cannot say.** Four nodes on one machine cannot show a lobby that needs slicing -- it never
would -- so what is measured is that the sliced path *works*: the topics are right, the advert reaches the slice, the
table forms and plays. The fifteen seconds X2 cost over X1 are the honest price of a network too small to have peers
in a founder's slice: the table was found by the question rather than by a broadcast, which is exactly what the
question is for, and what per-slice discovery in the DHT is for in a network large enough to slice for real.

**Guard.** `net::swarm::tests::the_peer_score_counts_refusals_and_not_traffic` (the rate terms are zero, the
library validates the params, and the settled-score arithmetic of the table above),
`net::lobby::tests::a_full_window_rotates_and_keeps_the_table_this_client_is_at` (a full window turns over by
first-seen, the held table survives both the bound and an expiry sweep, and goes back into the rotation when the
player leaves) and `::a_full_window_gives_up_only_so_many_rows_a_minute` (the pace applies only to a full window, a
minute has its own share, and a row already shown is refreshed whatever the pace).


## D-056 — the window asks for frames at a bounded rate, and the bound follows the rasteriser

**Decided 2026-09-14, the owner's ruling** (*"a co udělat limit fps na 25 snímků za vteřinu (zbytečná zátěž na GPU
teď), to není FPS online hra"*, then *"všeobecně optimalizovat GUI proti žraní GPU"* and *"a to samé pro CPU render
pro to GUI na strojích s nedosažitelnou GPU akcelerací"*).

1. **Twenty-five frames a second, and one place decides it.** `gui::table::paint_again` is the only way anything in
   this window asks to be drawn again; every animation clock goes through it -- the chips in flight, the badge that
   has just popped, the winner's blink, the seat clocks, the spinner in the lobby, the *Show cards* countdown, and
   the wake that comes back for the rest of a burst of events. Two of those used to call `request_repaint` outright,
   which is the display's own rate: at 144 Hz that is well over half a core of repaints for a chip sliding across a
   felt, and it reads exactly the same at 25.
2. **The number that matters is the count of repaints, not the frame rate**, and this project has already measured
   what one costs: about **4 ms** through a graphics driver and about **500 ms** on the software rasteriser
   (`main.rs`'s own table, and the 660 % of a core it once cost). So the cap cannot be one number:
   `FRAME` is 40 ms where there is a driver and `FRAME_SOFTWARE` is 250 ms where there is not -- asking a machine
   that needs half a second a frame for twenty-five of them is asking for twelve times what it has, and the next
   frame is then always due before the last is finished.
3. **A window nobody is looking at is asked for less** (`FRAME_UNFOCUSED`, five a second): a table left open behind
   another window still has a clock ticking and chips flying and nobody watching either. **A minimised window is
   asked for nothing at all** -- it has no pixels, and what it would have drawn is drawn when it comes back.
4. **The slow clocks are not sped up.** The cap is a floor on the interval, never a ceiling: a once-a-second clock
   stays once a second, and only what asked for *more* than the cap is slowed to it.
5. `main.rs` says which rasteriser it settled on (`drawing_without_a_gpu`) before the window opens. A process-wide
   fact decided once, rather than a parameter threaded through forty painting signatures.

**Guard.** `gui::table::tests::the_window_asks_for_frames_at_a_bounded_rate` (both caps, their order, that the
floor follows the rasteriser, and that a slow clock is not sped up).

## D-057 — the window says how its own way back to the table is going

**Decided 2026-09-14, the owner's ruling** (*"a v GUI aby byl uživatel informován hlášením o průběhu reconnectu, aby
stůl nevypadal zamrzlý"*).

1. **A table waiting on this client's own line shows every step of the way back**, over the felt where *Line down*
   was: the connection lost (or, at three seats or more, nobody at the table answering), the network back, the
   table's group again, the running hand followed while this seat was out of it, the sit-in asked at its end, and
   dealt in. Each step is done, under way or still to come; the one under way turns once a second, the panel says
   how long it has been, and a sentence under the steps says what the step under way waits on. *Back in the game*
   stays four seconds and goes.
2. **Why.** Between the line coming back and the seat being dealt in there can be a minute of things to wait for,
   and the felt showed none of them: *Line down* went and nothing replaced it (the far founder's return in
   `fe181646-3`: table reachable 243.5 s, dealt in from hand #21 after following hand #20 and a return vote -- a
   minute from its line coming back). A window that shows nothing for a minute looks frozen, and a player who thinks
   the table froze leaves it.
3. **Only this client's own way back.** At two seats nobody answering is as likely the opponent as this line, and
   that has its own question (`D-046`); there the panel starts only when the library says this client's own line is
   gone. The seats that are off the line are `S1-EI`'s panel, which the way back replaces while it is shown.
4. **From the node's own facts, not from its log lines**: `NodeEvent::TableReach` (whether any seat can be reached
   from here, on change), `SitInAsked` (this seat's own request), and `SessionResumed { member }` (a running hand
   taken up, dealt in or followed); with `ToxLine`, `SeatCertified` and `HandBegan` the window already had.
5. The panel repaints once a second, as *Line down* did, inside `D-056`'s budget.

**Guard.** `app::tests::the_way_back_is_shown_step_by_step_until_dealt_in_again` (the far founder's sequence, and a
short outage that put nobody out) and `app::tests::heads_up_the_way_back_waits_for_this_clients_own_line`.
`--table-preview --preview-rejoin` and `--preview-rejoin-back` draw it.

**Amended 2026-09-15 (`S1-FR`, the owner: *"chybí tam info okno, které má zobrazovat progress reconnectu"*).** A client started again with an unfinished game on record is on its way back from the seat it takes up again -- `Seated`, or `Hosting` for a founder back -- and the steps begin *Coming back after a restart* (done), then *Back in the table's group*, and go on as after a lost line until it is dealt in. The felt's own note is not drawn under the panel. **Guard.** `app::tests::a_client_back_after_a_restart_is_shown_its_way_back`.

## D-058 — the window says how the table's wait on a seat is going

**Decided 2026-09-14, the owner's ruling** (*"podobně uživatelsky hezké GUI okno z commitu a721ff7 bych chtěl mít i pro situace, kdy u
stolu, který čeká na nekomunikujícího peera, a pak přijde proces (hlasování atd.) na certifikaci"*).

1. **A seat the table waits on gets the same panel of steps as this client's own way back (`D-057`)**, in the place
   `S1-EI`'s sentences about the seats off the line had: the seat stopped answering, the hand waits on its clock
   (with the seconds while it is that seat's turn), the other seats agree to act for it (with the count), certified
   out and the hand goes on without it, back on the line -- and, if it comes back, its sit-in at the end of a hand,
   the seats agreeing to its return (with the count), and dealt in again. The title names the seat -- *Waiting for
